docs.title: Home
docs.text:
3 MIN READ Data Quality validation framework for Databricks

Neco DQ is a declarative data quality framework for Databricks, built on Spark and organized around the medallion architecture. You define checks in YAML, one set per layer, and the framework runs them, gates your pipeline on the result, and stores the history. The same configuration runs unchanged in a notebook, a scheduled Job, or a DLT pipeline.

Main features

  • ~35 built-in checks - medallion-aware: Bronze ingestion, Silver correctness, Gold reconciliation.
  • Policy engine - decides what blocks the pipeline vs what only warns, per suite and severity.
  • Great Expectations, integrated - run GE column contracts alongside native checks, in one report.
  • Custom suites - write your own checks in Python when the built-ins don't cover a rule.
  • Multi-environment profiles - one config targets dev, staging and prod via profile variables.
  • Slack alerts - send a summary of failures and warnings to a Slack channel per run.
  • Dashboard generation - build a Databricks AI/BI (Lakeview) dashboard on the DQ history table.
  • One report, one history - unified summary plus a Delta history table for trend analysis.

Philosophy

Every team has a different definition of "bad data". A missing field might be a hard pipeline blocker for one team and a non-critical warning for another. Neco DQ is built around that reality: the framework provides the checks, you decide what each one means.

Every check exposes three independent controls:

Parameter What it controls severity How the failure is classified (critical, error, warning, info) blocking Whether a failure stops the pipeline (exit_code=20) or only warns (exit_code=10) enabled Whether the check runs at all

On top of that, checks can be tagged and runs can be filtered by tag, so the same config can serve a full nightly run, a quick smoke test, and an on-demand critical-only check, without duplicating YAML.

Define once, adopt across teams. The checks, the execution engine, and the result contract live in one place and are maintained once. A team doesn't write or maintain data quality code, it writes a YAML config for its own tables and owns that config. Add a second team, or a tenth, and none of them reimplements freshness, uniqueness, or reconciliation logic: they reuse the same checks and inherit every fix and new capability. The effort of maintaining the framework is paid once, not once per team, which is where a shared platform pays off over data quality scripts copied from one pipeline to the next.

Data privacy by design. The framework reads your data to run checks, but never stores it. Every check computes statistics, counts, and aggregates on the Spark DataFrame and only the results (numbers, pass/fail status, query templates) are persisted to Delta. Row-level values never leave your environment.

This extends naturally to multi-environment deployments through profiles. You define a single suite and a single set of checks, then let each profile (dev, staging, prod) override the values that differ per environment: catalog names, thresholds, blocking flags, or entire policy sections, without duplicating config. The same freshness check can tolerate a 48-hour delay in dev and enforce a strict 2-hour window in production, all from one YAML file.

Get started

Getting Started Install, configure, and run your first data quality validation Installation Deploy the framework on Databricks, configure the wheel, and set up result storage

Test suites

Bronze Schema validation, null checks, and basic data integrity rules Silver Business rule validation and referential integrity checks Gold Aggregation accuracy, KPI validation, and cross-dataset consistency Profiling Statistical profiling and data distribution analysis Custom Suites Write your own data quality rules beyond the standard tiers Great Expectations Native Great Expectations integration for expectation-based validation

Guides

Database Setup Configure catalog, schema, and table connections Modular Config Split and compose configuration files across environments Running DQ Run validations with run_dq(): suites, selectors, tags, and profiles Data Filtering Scope validation to specific partitions, dates, or row subsets Profiles Multi-environment configuration with dev, staging, and prod profiles

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: 5 MIN READ Get Neco DQ running in minutes

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
pip install neco-dq-framework

Clusters with internet access can install straight from PyPI with the same command.

If your Databricks environment has no outbound internet, or you want to pin an exact version, host the wheel yourself on a Unity Catalog Volume. Download it from PyPI once:

pip download neco-dq-framework --no-deps -d ./wheelhouse

Upload the resulting .whl to a Volume your workspace can read, then install it:

%pip install /Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/wheelhouse/neco_dq_framework-X.Y.Z-py3-none-any.whl

docs.title: 2. Create Config
docs.text:
Save this as /path/bronze_suite.yaml:

bronze:
  tables:
    - catalog: your_catalog
      schema: your_schema
      table: your_table
      checks:
        freshness:
          enabled: true
          timestamp_column: batch_ingestion_at
          max_delay_hours: 24

        schema_drift:
          enabled: true
          expected_columns:
            project_id: string
            record_id: string

docs.title: 3. Run
docs.text:
from neco_dq.runner import run_dq

results = run_dq("/path/bronze_suite.yaml")

docs.title: Step 1: Create Configuration
docs.text:
For production, use the modular configuration structure:

/path/config/
├── global/
│   └── policy.yaml
└── suites/
    └── bronze/
        ├── suite.yaml
        └── test_groups/
            └── ingestion.yaml

policy.yaml:

dq_policy:
  block_test_suites:
    profiling: false
    bronze: true
    silver: true
    gold: true
    great_expectations: true

  alerts:
    slack:
      enabled: true

suite.yaml:

default_checks:
  record_count:
    enabled: true
    severity: warning
    blocking: false

  table_freshness:
    enabled: true
    severity: warning
    blocking: false
    max_staleness_days: 2

ingestion.yaml:

tables:
  - catalog: my_catalog
    schema: my_schema_bronze
    table: answers
    checks:
      mandatory_fields:
        enabled: true
        severity: critical
        blocking: true
        columns:
          - user_id
          - record_id
          - response_date

      schema_drift:
        enabled: true
        severity: critical
        blocking: true
        expected_columns:
          user_id: string
          record_id: string
          response_date: timestamp
          rating: integer

Configuration options

For simpler use cases, you can use a single YAML file. See Single-File Configuration. For multi-environment deployments (dev/staging/prod), see Profiles.

docs.title: Step 2: Run Validation
docs.text:
from neco_dq.runner import run_dq

results = run_dq(
    "/path/config/",
    run_suites=["bronze"]
)

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text: Exit Code Status Meaning 0 PASS All checks passed 10 WARN Non-blocking failures only 20 FAIL One or more blocking failures 99 SYSTEM_ERROR Invalid configuration or system error

docs.title: What if a check fails?
docs.text: A failing check doesn't just print FAIL: it attaches statistics and an investigation query template (never row values) so you can find the offending rows. See Debugging Failures for how to read failure_stats and investigation_query.

docs.title: Installation & Deployment
docs.text:
Installation options, terminal output, execution flow, failure policies, Databricks jobs, Declarative Pipelines, and security.

New to neco_dq?

Start with Getting Started for a 5-minute quick start.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Access to a Databricks workspace
  • Python >= 3.11

docs.title: Where to Find the Wheel
docs.text: Location Path Use Case PyPI neco-dq-framework pip install, local development Unity Catalog Volume /Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/wheelhouse/ Databricks jobs, notebooks, DLT pipelines

docs.title: Option 1: From PyPI
docs.text: pip install neco-dq-framework

docs.title: Option 2: From a Unity Catalog Volume
docs.text:
Hosting the wheel on a Volume is the usual choice for Databricks jobs, notebooks, and DLT pipelines. It works when the cluster has no outbound internet, and it lets you pin an exact version instead of resolving it from PyPI at install time.

First get the wheel. Download it from PyPI on any machine with internet access:

pip download neco-dq-framework --no-deps -d ./wheelhouse

This writes neco_dq_framework-X.Y.Z-py3-none-any.whl to ./wheelhouse. Upload that file to a Volume your workspace can read, then install it:

%pip install /Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/wheelhouse/neco_dq_framework-X.Y.Z-py3-none-any.whl

For Databricks Jobs, add the library in task configuration:

libraries:
  - whl: /Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/wheelhouse/neco_dq_framework-X.Y.Z-py3-none-any.whl

For classic (non-serverless) Declarative Pipelines, add the wheel under libraries:

{
  "libraries": [
    {"whl": "/Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/wheelhouse/neco_dq_framework-X.Y.Z-py3-none-any.whl"}
  ]
}

Serverless pipelines reject libraries.whl. Declare the wheel as an environment dependency instead:

{
  "environment": {
    "dependencies": [
      "/Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/wheelhouse/neco_dq_framework-X.Y.Z-py3-none-any.whl"
    ]
  }
}

Or install from a wheel uploaded to your Workspace:

%pip install --upgrade --force-reinstall \
  /Workspace/Users/your.email@example.com/libs/neco_dq_framework-X.Y.Z-py3-none-any.whl

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
import neco_dq
print(f"neco_dq version: {neco_dq.__version__}")

Flexibility for Teams

The wheel can be published to PyPI and/or a Unity Catalog Volume. Teams can:

  • Install from PyPI for local development or CI/CD pipelines
  • Use directly from a shared volume (always up-to-date)
  • Copy to a team-dedicated volume for version pinning or isolation
  • Upload to team Workspace for full control over updates

docs.title: Verbose Mode
docs.text:
Control output verbosity and Great Expectations progress bars with the verbose parameter:

from neco_dq.runner import run_dq

# Default: clean output, GE progress bars hidden
results = run_dq("/Workspace/config/")

# Verbose: debug logging, GE progress bars visible
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    verbose=True
)
verbose Log Level GE Progress Bars False (default) INFO Hidden True DEBUG Visible

When verbose mode is enabled:

  • Log level is set to DEBUG (shows ConfigResolver details)
  • Great Expectations progress bars are visible (via ProgressBarsConfig)
  • Additional internal details are logged

docs.title: Understanding Execution Flow
docs.text: At a high level, run_dq() resolves your config, runs the requested suites, applies the failure policy, then emits a summary, alerts and stored results, returning an exit code (0 / 10 / 20 / 99). The full step-by-step flow with diagram lives in Architecture → Execution Flow; the exit codes are covered under Failure Handling below.

docs.title: Failure Handling
docs.text:
Each check has two properties that control how failures affect the pipeline:

Property Values Effect severity warning, critical Informational only (appears in reports) blocking true, false Determines exit code

The framework has no defaults. Each team decides what should block and what should warn.

checks:
  freshness:
    enabled: true
    severity: critical
    blocking: true      # Exit 20 on failure

  record_count:
    enabled: true
    severity: warning
    blocking: false     # Exit 10 on failure (non-blocking)

Exit codes:

Code When 0 All checks passed 10 Only blocking: false checks failed 20 At least one blocking: true check failed

docs.title: Running as a Databricks Job
docs.text: For production deployments, run neco_dq as a scheduled Databricks Job.

docs.title: Job Configuration
docs.text:
Step 1: Reference the wheel

Use any of these options based on your team's preference:

Shared Volume (Recommended)Team VolumeTeam Workspace

Reference the wheel directly from a shared Unity Catalog Volume:

/Volumes/<catalog>/<schema>/wheelhouse/neco_dq_framework-X.Y.Z-py3-none-any.whl

Copy the wheel to your team's dedicated volume for version pinning:

/Volumes/<your_catalog>/<your_schema>/wheelhouse/neco_dq_framework-X.Y.Z-py3-none-any.whl

Upload the wheel to your team's Workspace folder:

/Workspace/Users/your.email@example.com/libs/neco_dq_framework-X.Y.Z-py3-none-any.whl

Step 2: Create entrypoint script

Save as /Workspace/Users/your.email@example.com/scripts/run_dq.py:

from neco_dq.runner import run_dq

def main():

    results = run_dq(
        "/feature/config/",
        run_suites=["bronze"]
    )

    print(results)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Step 3: Configure Databricks Job

Create a new Job with these settings:

Setting Value Task type Python wheel Environment Path to wheel (Volume or Workspace, see Step 1) Script Path to run_dq.py Cluster Select existing or create new Schedule Table Update Max retries 0 Timeout 30 minutes Email notifications On failure

docs.title: Running Inside a Declarative Pipeline
docs.text: You can run neco_dq inside a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline (formerly DLT) so the graph gates on data quality. The pattern is different from a Job: run_dq() cannot be a free-floating call, it has to live inside a dataset so the pipeline knows about it.

docs.title: The Pattern
docs.text:
Wrap run_dq() in a @dp.table that returns a DataFrame of results, and gate that dataset with a native expectation. One @dp.table becomes one node in the graph.

import json
from pyspark import pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql import Row
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, LongType
from neco_dq.runner import run_dq

CONFIG_REF = "/Workspace/Users/your.email@example.com/dq-config/"

RESULT_SCHEMA = StructType([
    StructField("suite", StringType()),
    StructField("status", StringType()),
    StructField("blocking_failures", LongType()),
    StructField("summary_json", StringType()),
])


@dp.table(name="my_catalog.my_schema.dq_results_bronze")
@dp.expect_all_or_fail({"no_blocking_dq_failures": "blocking_failures = 0"})
def dq_results_bronze():
    # Read the upstream tables so DQ runs after they materialize (see below).
    spark.read.table("my_catalog.my_schema.orders")
    spark.read.table("my_catalog.my_schema.customers")

    try:
        summary = run_dq(config_ref=CONFIG_REF, run_suites=["bronze"])
        rows = [
            Row(
                suite=name,
                status=str(s.get("status")),
                blocking_failures=int(s.get("blocking_failures", 0)),
                summary_json=json.dumps(s, default=str),
            )
            for name, s in summary.items()
        ]
    except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001
        # Capture the policy error as a row so the expectation fails the node,
        # not the analysis phase. See "Blocking failures" below.
        rows = [Row(suite="bronze", status="FAIL", blocking_failures=1,
                    summary_json=json.dumps({"blocking_error": str(e)}))]

    return spark.createDataFrame(rows, schema=RESULT_SCHEMA)

The @dp.expect_all_or_fail decorator turns the node red when a blocking failure lands, and green otherwise. An expectation always needs a dataset decorator (@dp.table or @dp.view): it cannot decorate a bare function on its own.

docs.title: Graph Granularity
docs.text:
The number of nodes in the graph equals the number of @dp.table definitions. Pick the granularity you want:

Granularity How Nodes in graph Per suite One @dp.table per suite, run_suites=["bronze"] One per suite Per table One @dp.table per table, selector={"bronze": ["orders"]} One per table Single node One @dp.table calling run_dq() for everything One, layer shown in the suite column

There is no way to get many graph nodes from a single table: "one table" and "many steps" are in conflict, because the count of @dp.table definitions drives both.

docs.title: Blocking Failures Turn the Node Red
docs.text:
run_dq() runs at graph-analysis time, before materialization. A blocking failure raises a RuntimeError, and if that propagates it aborts the whole update during analysis: every step shows as "not run", with no red node to point at.

The fix is in the pattern above. Catch the exception inside the function, emit a row with blocking_failures=1, and let @dp.expect_all_or_fail fail the node at materialization. Upstream data tables stay green, and only the DQ node turns red.

docs.title: Full-Refresh Ordering
docs.text:
run_dq() reads tables by their full Unity Catalog name, which does not register a pipeline dependency edge. On a full refresh the validation can run before the upstream tables exist, producing false record_count or freshness failures.

Read the upstream tables inside the function (the spark.read.table(...) calls in the example) so the pipeline orders the DQ node after them. Incremental runs against tables that already hold data are not affected.

docs.title: Service Principal and Security Model
docs.text: For production deployments, run neco_dq using a service principal with least-privilege access.

docs.title: Required Permissions
docs.text:
The service principal needs:

Resource Permission Purpose Source tables SELECT Read data for validation Metadata catalog/schema USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA Access metadata database History table SELECT, INSERT Write execution results Alerts table SELECT, INSERT Write alerts (if enabled)

docs.title: Security Best Practices
docs.text:
• No write permissions: Service principal should NEVER have INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE on source data
  • Dedicated metadata catalog: Use separate catalog/schema for DQ metadata, not production catalogs
  • Audit trail: All executions are logged with service principal identity in dq_test_history
  • Rotate credentials: If using personal access tokens, rotate them regularly

See: Database Setup for metadata table configuration.

docs.title: Result Persistence and Reporting
docs.text: The framework persists validation results to Delta tables for historical tracking and reporting.

docs.title: Required Setup
docs.text:
Before running validations in production, you need to create metadata tables to persist execution results:

  1. dq_test_history - Stores ALL check results (passed and failed)
  2. dq_test_alerts_log - Stores ONLY failures and warnings (optional)

See: Database Setup for complete setup instructions, table schemas, and customization options.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Where Neco DQ is heading. This page describes direction, not commitments. Items and their order can change, and nothing here has a fixed release date.

How to read this page

Every future item follows the same two rules the framework already lives by: it is opt-in, and it is backward compatible. A run that does not adopt a new feature behaves exactly as it does today. Where an item is still a proposal, its own page (or this section) says so.

docs.title: Horizons
docs.text: Horizon Meaning Available today Shipped and documented. Safe to build on. Planned A design direction we intend to build. Details may still change. Exploring Early design under discussion. No commitment, no timeline.

docs.title: Available today
docs.text:
The current release is a complete data quality framework. In short:

  • Around 35 built-in checks across Bronze, Silver, and Gold.
  • A policy engine that decides, per suite and severity, what blocks a pipeline and what only warns.
  • Great Expectations column contracts running alongside native checks in one report.
  • Custom Python suites for rules the built-ins do not cover.
  • Multi-environment profiles so one config targets dev, staging, and prod.
  • Slack alerts, a Lakeview dashboard, and a Delta history table for trends.

See the home page for the full feature list and Getting Started to run the framework.

docs.title: Parameter naming consistency
docs.text: Some parameters carry different names for the same idea across suites (for example, the column a freshness check reads). The plan is to converge on one name per concept, keeping the old names as accepted aliases so existing configs keep working without change.

docs.title: Exploring
docs.text: These are under active design in the open. They are not scheduled, and the notes below describe intent, not a shipping feature.

docs.title: Optional AI assistance
docs.text:
An optional, opt-in layer that helps teams author and understand data quality, without changing how the engine runs. The design is built around a few fixed rules:

  • Off by default. A team that does nothing gets no AI and no added cost. It turns on only through explicit configuration.
  • Privacy first. Row-level values never leave the environment. The default target is a model running inside the workspace, and features that would touch data stay in-workspace unless a team explicitly opts into an external target.
  • Grounded, not trusted. Anything the model generates (a suite config) is checked against the framework's own machine-readable capability description before it is used. Anything it explains (a failure) is advisory text, never a gate.

The candidate uses, roughly in order of how ready they are:

Use What it does Failure explanation Turns failed-check metadata into a plain-language likely cause, attached to the summary. Safe metadata only. Suite generation Proposes a suite config from a table's profile or from a natural-language request, then validates it before writing. Semantic checks Runs classification or generation as an in-workspace SQL column, for rules that need to read text meaning. Config repair Given validation errors on a config, proposes a corrected one and re-checks it.

docs.title: Portable execution beyond Databricks
docs.text: Today the engine runs on Spark and Databricks. We are exploring a portable execution layer so the same checks can run against other SQL engines, locally, or in CI, with credentials and model access resolved per environment rather than assumed to be Databricks.

docs.title: Data contracts
docs.text: A longer-term direction: schema-as-code, so a table's shape and expectations are declared once and checked as a contract, with notification when a change would affect consumers. Still at the design stage.

docs.title: Principles that will not change
docs.text:
Whatever lands, these hold:

  • Existing runs keep working. New features are opt-in and backward compatible.
  • Row-level values never leave your environment.
  • The result contract stays stable, so history and dashboards remain comparable over time.
  • AI, if adopted, is advisory or validated. It never gates a pipeline on unchecked output.

docs.title: Have input?
docs.text: Priorities are shaped by real use. Open an issue or start a discussion on GitHub with the checks, integrations, or workflows you need.

docs.title: Debug Experience
docs.text: When a check fails, you need to quickly understand what went wrong and how to investigate. The Debug Experience provides structured information at multiple layers.

docs.title: Result Layers
docs.text:
Every check result includes these layers:

Layer Purpose When Present details Human-readable summary Always failure_stats Aggregate statistics Only on FAIL investigation_query SQL template for debugging Only on FAIL execution Performance context Always

docs.title: details
docs.text:
A concise message (~60 chars) that tells you what happened at a glance.

PASS examples: 

Record count OK: 5000 rows
All 5000 keys unique
Data age 2h within 24h limit

FAIL examples: 

Found 50 duplicate keys (5.0%)
Data age 48h exceeds 24h limit
Missing 3 required columns

docs.title: failure_stats
docs.text:
Aggregate statistics about the failure. Never contains row values or PII.

{
  "failure_type": "duplicate_key",
  "affected_columns": ["order_id"],
  "failure_count": 47,
  "total_rows_checked": 50000,
  "failure_percentage": 0.094,
  "distribution": {
    "duplicates_2": 30,
    "duplicates_3_5": 12,
    "duplicates_6_plus": 5
  },
  "diagnostic": {
    "max_duplicates_per_key": 8,
    "avg_duplicates_per_key": 2.4
  }
}

docs.title: investigation_query
docs.text:
A SQL template you can run to find the failing rows. The query is parameterized with your table and filter context.

-- Find duplicate keys
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) as cnt
FROM catalog.schema.orders
WHERE batch_date = '2026-06-01'
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY cnt DESC
LIMIT 100

docs.title: execution
docs.text:
Context about how the check ran: timing, row counts, filters applied, table info, and profile context.

{
  "duration_ms": 1234,
  "started_at": "2026-06-15T10:30:00Z",
  "rows_scanned": 1000000,
  "rows_after_filter": 50000,
  "filters_applied": {
    "row_filter": "status = 'active'",
    "partition_filter": {
      "date": "2026-06-01"
    }
  },
  "table": {
    "catalog": "analytics_prod",
    "schema": "silver",
    "name": "orders"
  },
  "profile": {
    "name": "prod",
    "target_catalog": "analytics_prod"
  }
}

Fields:

Field Description duration_ms Check execution time in milliseconds started_at ISO 8601 timestamp when check started rows_scanned Total rows in source table rows_after_filter Rows remaining after filters filters_applied Filters that were applied (row_filter, partition_filter, time_window) table Primary table info (catalog, schema, name) secondary_tables Other tables read (for cross-table checks) profile Profile context (only present when profiles are used)

The profile field is only present when running with an active profile (not when using single-file configs without profiles).

docs.title: Security Guarantees
docs.text:
The Debug Experience is designed to never expose sensitive data:

Data Type Stored? Reason Counts/percentages Yes Aggregate statistics Distribution buckets Yes Statistical summaries Column names Yes Schema metadata Query templates Yes No data embedded Row values Never Direct PII risk Primary keys Never Can be PII (SSN, email) Sample rows Never Contains values

docs.title: Quick Triage
docs.text:
Start with details to understand what failed:

Found 50 duplicate keys (5.0%)

docs.title: Assess Severity
docs.text:
Check failure_stats to understand the scale:

{
  "failure_count": 50,
  "total_rows_checked": 1000,
  "failure_percentage": 5.0,
  "distribution": {
    "duplicates_2": 45,
    "duplicates_3_plus": 5
  }
}

Most duplicates appear only twice (45 keys), with 5 keys having 3+ duplicates.

docs.title: Investigate
docs.text:
Run the investigation_query in Databricks to find the actual failing rows:

SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) as cnt
FROM catalog.schema.orders
WHERE batch_date = '2026-06-01'
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY cnt DESC

docs.title: Understand Context
docs.text:
Check execution if results seem unexpected:

{
  "rows_scanned": 1000000,
  "rows_after_filter": 1000,
  "filters_applied": {
    "row_filter": "status = 'pending'"
  },
  "table": {
    "catalog": "analytics_prod",
    "schema": "silver",
    "name": "orders"
  },
  "profile": {
    "name": "prod",
    "target_catalog": "analytics_prod"
  }
}

Only 1000 rows were checked due to the filter. The 5% failure rate is within those filtered rows. The profile field confirms this ran against the prod environment.

docs.title: Duplicate Checks (idempotency, uniqueness)
docs.text:
{
  "failure_type": "duplicate_key",
  "affected_columns": ["order_id"],
  "distribution": {
    "duplicates_2": 30,
    "duplicates_3_5": 12,
    "duplicates_6_plus": 5
  }
}

docs.title: Null Checks (mandatory_fields)
docs.text:
{
  "failure_type": "null_value",
  "affected_columns": ["email", "phone"],
  "null_distribution": {
    "email": 100,
    "phone": 56,
    "both_null": 23
  }
}

docs.title: Referential Integrity
docs.text:
{
  "failure_type": "orphan_reference",
  "affected_columns": ["product_id"],
  "reference_info": {
    "target_table": "catalog.products",
    "target_column": "id"
  },
  "diagnostic": {
    "distinct_orphan_fks": 45
  }
}

docs.title: Compare Metric (grouped)
docs.text:
{
  "failure_type": "metric_mismatch",
  "group_columns": ["account_id", "date"],
  "deviation_stats": {
    "max_deviation_pct": 50.0,
    "avg_deviation_pct": 15.3
  }
}

docs.title: Querying Debug Data
docs.text:
Debug layers are stored in the history table. Query them for analysis:

SELECT
  check_name,
  details,
  failure_stats,
  investigation_query
FROM dq_test_history
WHERE passed = false
  AND run_timestamp > current_date() - 7
ORDER BY run_timestamp DESC

Parse failure_stats JSON for aggregations:

SELECT
  check_name,
  get_json_object(failure_stats, '$.failure_type') as failure_type,
  get_json_object(failure_stats, '$.failure_count') as failure_count,
  get_json_object(failure_stats, '$.failure_percentage') as failure_pct
FROM dq_test_history
WHERE passed = false

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text: Neco DQ Framework is built as a modular, registry-driven platform for data quality validation. This page explains the system architecture, components, and design principles.

docs.title: Mental Model: Kernel + Plugins
docs.text:
Think of Neco DQ Framework as an operating system for data quality:

Component Role Responsibility Analogy Orchestrator Lifecycle & ordering Coordinates execution, manages state Kernel Test Suites Compute validations Execute tests, collect metrics Plugins Policy Determine consequences Evaluate pass/fail, decide exit codes Judge Summary Aggregate & format Build reports, format output Narrator Alerts Notify stakeholders Send Slack messages, log events Messengers

The orchestrator acts as the kernel that loads and coordinates plugins (test suites), while other components provide specialized services.

docs.title: System Components
docs.text: neco_dq consists of these core components:

docs.title: 1. Runner
docs.text:
Purpose: Entry point for executing validations

File: neco_dq/runner.py

Responsibilities: - Parse command-line arguments or API calls - Initialize Spark session (if not provided) - Invoke config resolver - Call orchestrator - Return results

Interface:

def run_dq(
    config_ref: str,
    profile: str | None = None,
    run_suites: Iterable[str] | None = None,
    exclude_suites: Iterable[str] | None = None,
    selector: dict[str, list[str]] | None = None,
    tags: list[str] | None = None,
    custom_suite_files: str | list[str] | None = None,
    verbose: bool = False,
)

docs.title: 2. Config Resolver
docs.text:
Purpose: Load and interpret configuration files

File: neco_dq/config/config_resolver.py

Responsibilities: - Detect configuration mode (modular, single-file, template) - Load YAML files from directories or single files - Expand templates using registry - Validate configuration schema - Return normalized configuration objects

Key Principle: Suites never parse YAML. Config Resolver handles all configuration interpretation.

docs.title: 3. Orchestrator
docs.text:
Purpose: Coordinate test suite execution

File: neco_dq/core/orchestrators/dq_orchestrator.py

Responsibilities: - Load test suites from registry - Execute suites in correct order - Collect results from each suite - Pass results to policy engine - Coordinate summary and alerts

Critical Rules: - Never computes metrics - Never parses YAML - Never applies business logic - Coordinates only

docs.title: 4. Test Suites
docs.text:
Purpose: Execute validation tests on datasets

Files: - neco_dq/test_suites/bronze/bronze_dq_test_suite.py - neco_dq/test_suites/silver/silver_dq_test_suite.py - neco_dq/test_suites/gold/gold_dq_test_suite.py - neco_dq/test_suites/ge/ge_dq_test_suite.py - neco_dq/test_suites/profiling/profiling_dq_test_suite.py

Responsibilities: - Load tables from Spark - Execute configured tests - Compute observed metrics - Compare against expected values using operators - Return standardized results

Critical Rules: - Stateless (no side effects) - Compute only (no alerts, no policy) - No file access (config comes from orchestrator) - No dependencies on other suites

docs.title: 5. Registry
docs.text:
Purpose: Discover and load test suites

File: neco_dq/core/registry/test_suite_registry.py

Responsibilities: - Register suite classes with unique names - Provide lookup by suite name - Validate suite implementations - Prevent naming conflicts

docs.title: 6. Policy Engine
docs.text:
Purpose: Evaluate test results and determine consequences

File: neco_dq/core/policy/dq_failure_policy.py

Responsibilities: - Evaluate each test result (PASS/FAIL/WARN) - Apply severity levels (CRITICAL, WARNING) - Respect blocking flags - Determine exit codes - Decide whether to fail fast or continue

Execution: Runs strictly AFTER suite execution, never during.

docs.title: 7. Summary Engine
docs.text:
Purpose: Aggregate and format results

Files: - neco_dq/core/summary/summary_engine.py - neco_dq/core/summary/terminal_logger.py

Responsibilities: - Aggregate results across all suites - Calculate statistics (pass rate, totals) - Format output for terminal display - Generate structured summaries for programmatic access

Input: Normalized result records from suites

Output: Human-readable reports and structured data

docs.title: 8. Alerts
docs.text:
Purpose: Notify stakeholders of validation results

File: neco_dq/core/alerts/slack_alerts.py

Responsibilities: - Send Slack messages on failures or warnings - Format alert messages with test details - Handle alert channel configuration - Respect enable/disable flags

Trigger: Post-policy evaluation

docs.title: 9. Result Persistence
docs.text:
Purpose: Store validation results for audit and analysis

File: neco_dq/core/io/result_writer.py

Responsibilities: - Write results to Delta Lake tables - Persist detailed test records - Store execution metadata - Enable historical analysis

docs.title: Execution Flow
docs.text:
Here's the complete end-to-end flow when you run run_dq():

flowchart TB
    subgraph Step1["1. Runner"]
        R1[Parse arguments]
        R2[Initialize Spark]
    end

    subgraph Step2["2. Config Resolver"]
        C1[Detect config mode]
        C2[Load YAML files]
        C3[Expand templates]
        C4[Validate schema]
        C5[Return normalized config]
    end

    subgraph Step3["3. Orchestrator"]
        O1[Load suites from registry]
        O2[Filter by run_suites]
        O3[Execute each suite]
    end

    subgraph Step4["4. Test Suites"]
        Bronze["Bronze Suite<br/>Load → Test → Compute → Persist → Return"]
        Silver["Silver Suite<br/>Load → Test → Compute → Persist → Return"]
        Gold["Gold Suite<br/>Load → Test → Compute → Persist → Return"]
        Storage["Result Storage<br/>Delta Lake (written during execution)"]
    end

    subgraph Step5["5. Summary Engine"]
        S1[Aggregate results]
        S2[Calculate statistics]
        S3[Format + log reports]
    end

    subgraph Step6["6. Policy Engine"]
        P1[Evaluate PASS/FAIL/WARN]
        P2[Apply severity levels]
        P3[Determine exit code]
        P4[Send Slack alerts]
    end

    Step1 --> Step2
    Step2 --> Step3
    Step3 --> Bronze
    Step3 --> Silver
    Step3 --> Gold
    Bronze --> Storage
    Silver --> Storage
    Gold --> Storage
    Step4 --> Step5
    Step5 --> Step6

docs.title: Ownership by Layer
docs.text:
Each component has clear ownership and should never cross boundaries:

Layer Owns Never Does Orchestrator Lifecycle & ordering Compute metrics, parse YAML, apply business logic Config Resolver Configuration interpretation Execute tests, apply policy Test Suites Compute validations Trigger alerts, read files, apply policy Policy Engine Failure semantics Compute metrics, format output Summary Engine Aggregate & format Apply policy, execute tests Alerts Notify stakeholders Determine failures, execute tests Result Persistence Store results Determine failures, execute tests

docs.title: Non-Negotiable Architecture Rules
docs.text: These principles ensure the framework remains maintainable, extensible, and deterministic:

docs.title: 1. Orchestrator Purity
docs.text:
The orchestrator never: - Computes metrics - Parses YAML - Applies business logic

It only: - Coordinates execution - Manages lifecycle - Delegates to specialized components

docs.title: 2. Suite Statelessness
docs.text:
Test suites must be: - Stateless (no side effects) - Compute-only (no I/O operations) - Independent (no dependencies on other suites)

Test suites never: - Trigger alerts - Apply policy logic - Read configuration files - Access external systems

docs.title: 3. Policy Post-Execution
docs.text:
Policy evaluation runs strictly AFTER suite execution.

Never evaluate policy during test execution.

docs.title: 4. Result Contract
docs.text: All suites must emit standardized results with required fields. See Debug Experience for the result structure including details, failure_stats, investigation_query, and execution.

docs.title: 5. Registry Authority
docs.text: Suites are loaded exclusively through the registry.

docs.title: 6. Generalization Requirement
docs.text:
All checks, metrics, and helpers must be: - Generic and reusable across any dataset - Named to describe behavior, not business cases - Parameterized via configuration, not hardcoded

Good: array_is_sorted, value_in_range, column_not_null

Bad: price_rating_sorted, client_x_validation

docs.title: Determinism Requirement
docs.text:
neco_dq guarantees deterministic execution:

Same input + Same config = Same output

This means: - No randomness - No time-dependent behavior (unless explicitly configured) - No external dependencies that can change - Reproducible results for audit and debugging

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Now that you understand the architecture:

  • Configuration: Learn about Modular Config
  • Test Suites: Explore Bronze, Silver, Gold, or Great Expectations

docs.title: Compare Metric Reference
docs.text:
The compare_metric check is a generic validation tool that compares observed values computed from your data against expected values from various sources.

When to Use

Use compare_metric when you need to:

  • Validate aggregations (sums, counts, averages)
  • Compare metrics across tables
  • Enforce business thresholds
  • Validate statistical calculations
  • Check array field values
  • Verify ranking algorithms (Kendall's W, Borda Count)

docs.title: Basic Syntax
docs.text:
compare_metric:
  enabled: true
  severity: error
  blocking: true
  name: my_metric_check        # Optional: descriptive name

  observed:                     # REQUIRED: What to measure
    type: <metric_type>
    # ... metric-specific parameters

  # CHOOSE ONE: static value OR dynamic expected
  value: 100                    # Option 1: Compare to static value
  expected:                     # Option 2: Compare to dynamic value
    type: <resolver_type>
    # ... resolver-specific parameters

  operator: "=="                # Comparison operator
  tolerance_abs: 0.01               # Optional: for approximate comparisons

Key Aliases

This reference uses observed and expected. The following legacy aliases are still accepted:

  • observed or metric: defines the observed value
  • expected or expected_from: defines the dynamic expected value

docs.title: Observed Metrics
docs.text: The observed section defines what value to compute from your data.

docs.title: count
docs.text:
Counts rows in the DataFrame.

observed:
  type: count

docs.title: aggregate
docs.text:
Applies a Spark aggregation function.

Parameter Required Description column Yes Column to aggregate function Yes sum, avg, count, countDistinct where No SQL filter expression group_by No Columns for grouping 
observed:
  type: aggregate
  column: amount
  function: sum
  where: "status = 'completed'"
  group_by:
    - order_id

docs.title: column_value
docs.text:
Extracts a single column value (or grouped values).

Parameter Required Description column Yes Column to extract where No SQL filter expression group_by No Columns for grouping 
observed:
  type: column_value
  column: total_responses
  group_by:
    - order_id
    - product_id

docs.title: sql
docs.text:
Executes a raw SQL query.

observed:
  type: sql
  query: "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {catalog}.{schema}.{table} WHERE status = 'active'"

Placeholders

Use {catalog}, {schema}, {table} to reference the current table.

docs.title: size_array
docs.text:
Counts elements in an array column.

observed:
  type: size_array
  column: items
  group_by:
    - order_id

docs.title: sum_array_field
docs.text:
Sums a specific field within array elements.

Parameter Required Description column Yes Array column field Yes Field to sum within array path No Path for nested arrays value_type No Cast type (int, double) group_by No Columns for grouping 
observed:
  type: sum_array_field
  column: choices
  field: choice_pct
  value_type: double
  group_by:
    - order_id
    - product_id

docs.title: array_stats
docs.text:
Computes statistical measures from array field values.

Parameter Required Description column Yes Array column field Yes Field containing numeric values stat Yes Statistical measure (see below) weight No Field for weighted calculations path No Path for nested arrays (e.g., ranks) item_group_by No Match array elements (e.g., item_code\|item_label) median_method No For median: discrete, lower, upper, continuous group_by No Columns for grouping

Supported stat values:

Stat Description mean Average (weighted if weight specified) median Median value (configurable method) std Sample standard deviation min Minimum value max Maximum value ci_95_low 95% confidence interval lower bound ci_95_high 95% confidence interval upper bound

Example: Weighted Mean

observed:
  type: array_stats
  column: rating_levels
  field: rating_value
  weight: rating_count
  stat: mean
  group_by:
    - order_id
    - product_id

Example: Median with Method

observed:
  type: array_stats
  column: rating_levels
  field: rating_value
  stat: median
  median_method: lower
  group_by:
    - order_id
    - product_id

Example: Nested Array Stats

observed:
  type: array_stats
  column: items
  path: ranks                    # Navigate to nested 'ranks' array
  field: rank_position
  weight: rank_count
  item_group_by: item_code|item_label
  stat: mean
  group_by:
    - order_id
    - product_id

docs.title: kendall_w
docs.text:
Computes Kendall's W coefficient of concordance for ranking data.

Parameter Required Description column Yes Array column with ranking data rank_sum_field No Field for mean rank (default: mean_rank) appearances_field No Field for rater count (default: item_appearances_n) label No Expected consensus label (e.g., strong, moderate) label_column No Column containing expected label per group min_raters No Minimum raters required (default: 2) thresholds No Custom threshold values for labels group_by No Columns for grouping

Default Thresholds:

Label Threshold strong >= 0.9 moderate >= 0.7 fair >= 0.5 weak >= 0.3 low >= 0.2 none >= 0.0

Example: Basic Kendall W

observed:
  type: kendall_w
  column: items
  rank_sum_field: mean_rank
  appearances_field: item_appearances_n
  group_by:
    - order_id
    - product_id

Example: With Label Validation

observed:
  type: kendall_w
  column: items
  label_column: kendall_w_label    # Validate against expected label
  min_raters: 1                     # Allow single-rater
  thresholds:                       # Custom 3-level system
    strong: 0.5
    moderate: 0.3
    low: 0.0
  group_by:
    - order_id
    - product_id

docs.title: borda_count
docs.text:
Computes Borda Count scores for ranking data.

Parameter Required Description column Yes Array column with ranking items ranks_field Yes Field containing ranks array rank_position_field Yes Field for rank position within ranks rank_count_field Yes Field for vote count at each rank item_id_field Yes Field(s) identifying items (e.g., item_code\|item_label) fields No Output fields to include group_by No Columns for grouping 
observed:
  type: borda_count
  column: items
  ranks_field: ranks
  rank_position_field: rank_position
  rank_count_field: rank_count
  item_id_field: "item_code|item_label"
  fields: [item_id, borda_points, borda_norm_pct]
  group_by:
    - order_id
    - product_id

docs.title: Expected Resolvers
docs.text: The expected section defines where to get the expected value.

docs.title: static (using value)
docs.text:
Compare to a literal value.

value: 100.00
operator: "=="

docs.title: aggregate
docs.text:
Compute aggregation from another table.

Parameter Required Description catalog No Target catalog schema No Target schema table No Target table column Yes Column to aggregate function Yes sum, avg, count, countDistinct where No SQL filter expression group_by No Columns for grouping 
expected:
  type: aggregate
  catalog: my_catalog
  schema: my_schema
  table: source_table
  column: transaction_id
  function: count
  where: "type = 'single_choice'"
  group_by:
    - order_id

docs.title: sql
docs.text:
Execute a raw SQL query.

expected:
  type: sql
  query: "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM catalog.schema.table WHERE status = 'active'"

docs.title: column_value
docs.text:
Extract column value from a table.

Parameter Required Description catalog No Target catalog schema No Target schema table No Target table column Yes Column to extract where No SQL filter expression group_by No Columns for grouping 
expected:
  type: column_value
  catalog: my_catalog
  schema: my_schema
  table: summary_table
  column: expected_mean
  group_by:
    - order_id
    - product_id

docs.title: array_field_value
docs.text:
Extract values from array field elements.

Parameter Required Description catalog No Target catalog schema No Target schema table No Target table column Yes Array column field Yes* Single field to extract fields Yes* Multiple fields to extract item_group_by No Match array elements by field(s) group_by No Columns for grouping

*Use either field or fields, not both.

expected:
  type: array_field_value
  catalog: my_catalog
  schema: my_schema
  table: summary_ranking
  column: items
  fields: [borda_points, borda_norm_pct]
  item_group_by: "item_code|item_label"
  group_by:
    - order_id
    - product_id

docs.title: Operators
docs.text: Operator Description Tolerance Support == Exact equality No != Not equal No > Greater than No >= Greater or equal No < Less than No <= Less or equal No ~ Approximate equality Yes (absolute) within_pct Within percentage Yes (percentage) in Value in collection No not_in Value not in collection No between Value in range [min, max] No

docs.title: Using Tolerance
docs.text:
For approximate comparisons with floating-point values:

operator: "~"
tolerance_abs: 0.01  # Absolute tolerance: |observed - expected| <= 0.01

operator: "within_pct"
tolerance_abs: 5.0   # With within_pct the value is a percentage: difference <= 5%

docs.title: Group By
docs.text:
Use group_by to perform row-level comparisons across grouped data.

Important: When using group_by:

  • Both observed and expected must have matching group_by columns
  • Group keys are compared as string tuples
  • All groups must pass for the check to succeed
compare_metric:
  enabled: true
  observed:
    type: aggregate
    column: total
    function: sum
    group_by:
      - order_id
      - product_id

  expected:
    type: column_value
    catalog: my_catalog
    schema: my_schema
    table: reference
    column: expected_total
    group_by:
      - order_id
      - product_id

  operator: "=="

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Threshold Check
docs.text:
Verify total amount exceeds minimum.

compare_metric:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true

  observed:
    type: aggregate
    column: amount
    function: sum

  value: 100000
  operator: ">="

docs.title: Example 2: Cross-Table Count Comparison
docs.text:
Verify row counts match between tables.

compare_metric:
  enabled: true
  severity: error
  name: responses_count_match

  observed:
    type: count

  expected:
    type: aggregate
    catalog: my_catalog
    schema: silver
    table: source_responses
    column: "*"
    function: count
    where: "type = 'single_choice'"

  operator: "=="

docs.title: Example 3: Grouped Metric Validation
docs.text:
Verify aggregated values match reference table per group.

compare_metric:
  enabled: true
  severity: error
  name: revenue_per_region

  observed:
    type: aggregate
    column: revenue
    function: sum
    group_by:
      - region
      - quarter

  expected:
    type: column_value
    catalog: my_catalog
    schema: gold
    table: revenue_targets
    column: target_revenue
    group_by:
      - region
      - quarter

  operator: ">="

docs.title: Example 4: Array Field Sum Equals 100%
docs.text:
Verify percentages in array sum to 100.

compare_metric:
  enabled: true
  severity: error
  name: percentage_sum_100

  observed:
    type: sum_array_field
    column: choices
    field: choice_pct
    value_type: double
    group_by:
      - order_id
      - product_id

  value: 100.00
  operator: "~"
  tolerance_abs: 0.01

docs.title: Example 5: Weighted Mean from Array
docs.text:
Validate weighted mean calculation.

compare_metric:
  enabled: true
  severity: error
  name: rating_mean

  observed:
    type: array_stats
    column: rating_levels
    field: rating_value
    weight: rating_count
    stat: mean
    group_by:
      - order_id
      - product_id

  expected:
    type: column_value
    catalog: my_catalog
    schema: gold
    table: summary_rating
    column: mean
    group_by:
      - order_id
      - product_id

  operator: "~"
  tolerance_abs: 0.001

docs.title: Example 6: Kendall W Consensus Validation
docs.text:
Validate ranking consensus coefficient and label.

compare_metric:
  enabled: true
  severity: error
  name: kendall_consensus

  observed:
    type: kendall_w
    column: items
    rank_sum_field: mean_rank
    appearances_field: item_appearances_n
    label_column: kendall_w_label
    min_raters: 1
    thresholds:
      strong: 0.5
      moderate: 0.3
      low: 0.0
    group_by:
      - order_id
      - product_id

  expected:
    type: column_value
    catalog: my_catalog
    schema: gold
    table: summary_ranking
    column: kendall_w
    group_by:
      - order_id
      - product_id

  operator: "~"
  tolerance_abs: 0.01

docs.title: Example 7: Borda Count Validation
docs.text:
Validate Borda Count ranking scores.

compare_metric:
  enabled: true
  severity: error
  name: verify_borda_count

  observed:
    type: borda_count
    column: items
    ranks_field: ranks
    rank_position_field: rank_position
    rank_count_field: rank_count
    item_id_field: "item_code|item_label"
    fields: [item_id, borda_points, borda_norm_pct]
    group_by:
      - order_id
      - product_id

  expected:
    type: array_field_value
    catalog: my_catalog
    schema: gold
    table: summary_ranking
    column: items
    fields: [borda_points, borda_norm_pct]
    item_group_by: "item_code|item_label"
    group_by:
      - order_id
      - product_id

  operator: "=="

docs.title: Example 8: SQL-Based Validation
docs.text:
Use raw SQL for complex queries.

compare_metric:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  name: active_users_count

  observed:
    type: count

  expected:
    type: sql
    query: |
      SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)
      FROM my_catalog.silver.user_sessions
      WHERE session_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 30 DAYS
        AND status = 'active'

  operator: ">="

docs.title: Result Output
docs.text:
Check results include detailed information:

check_name: compare_metric
name: rating_mean
passed: true
details: observed=4.52; expected=4.52; operator=~; tolerance=0.001

For grouped comparisons with failures:

check_name: compare_metric
name: rating_mean
passed: false
details: Found 3/100 groups failing; group=('order_1', 'prod_5'): observed=4.2, expected=4.8; ...

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text: Issue Cause Solution "No matching groups" Group keys don't match Ensure group_by columns exist in both sources Type mismatch Comparing incompatible types Check value_type for arrays Tolerance not working Using == instead of ~ Use ~ operator with tolerance_abs Empty results Filter too restrictive Check where conditions

docs.title: Debugging Tips
docs.text:
1. Start simple: Test with type: count and static value first
  2. Check group alignment: Ensure group_by columns match exactly
  3. Use named checks: Add name for easier identification in results
  4. Test tolerance: For floating-point comparisons, always use ~ with tolerance_abs

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Silver Suite - Silver layer checks
  • Gold Suite - Gold layer checks
  • Data Filtering - Filter data before validation
  • Modular Config - Configuration structure

docs.title: Data Filtering
docs.text:
Data filtering allows you to run DQ checks on a subset of your data. This is useful for:

  • Validating only the most recent partitions
  • Testing specific data segments
  • Reducing compute costs on large tables
  • Incremental data quality validation

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The framework supports two types of filters:

Filter Type Purpose Scope partition_filter Filter on partition columns (optimized) Partition pruning row_filter SQL WHERE expression for any column Row-level filtering

Both filters can be configured at suite level (defaults) or table level (overrides).

docs.title: Partition Filter
docs.text: Partition filters use Delta table partition pruning to keep scans fast.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
tables:
  - catalog: my_catalog
    schema: my_schema
    table: events
    partition_filter:
      date: "2024-01-15"

docs.title: Multiple Columns
docs.text:
partition_filter:
  year: 2024
  month: 1

Generated SQL: year = 2024 AND month = 1

docs.title: Auto-Discovery (Recommended)
docs.text: The framework can automatically discover partition columns and filter on the latest values.

docs.title: Latest Single Partition
docs.text:
partition_filter:
  auto: true

This will: 1. Query table metadata for partition columns 2. Find the maximum value for each partition column 3. Filter data to only include the latest partition

docs.title: Latest N Partitions
docs.text:
partition_filter:
  auto_latest: 7  # Last 7 partitions

Useful for validating a rolling window of recent data.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The framework validates that partition_filter columns are actual partition columns:

  • If a non-partition column is used, a warning is included in the check details
  • The filter still executes, but without partition pruning optimization

docs.title: Row Filter
docs.text: Row filters apply SQL WHERE expressions to filter rows after partition pruning.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
tables:
  - catalog: my_catalog
    schema: my_schema
    table: orders
    row_filter: "status = 'COMPLETED'"

docs.title: Complex Expressions
docs.text: row_filter: "amount > 0 AND created_at >= '2024-01-01'"

docs.title: Combined with Partition Filter
docs.text:
tables:
  - catalog: my_catalog
    schema: my_schema
    table: events
    partition_filter:
      date: "2024-01-15"
    row_filter: "event_type = 'purchase'"

Execution order: 1. Partition filter applied first (partition pruning) 2. Row filter applied second (row-level filtering)

docs.title: Suite-Level Defaults
docs.text: Define filters once at suite level and apply to all tables.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
silver:
  defaults:
    partition_filter:
      auto: true  # All tables use latest partition
    row_filter: "is_valid = true"

  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema
      table: orders
      # Inherits: partition_filter.auto=true, row_filter="is_valid = true"

    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema
      table: payments
      partition_filter:
        date: "2024-01-15"  # Override suite default
      # Still inherits: row_filter="is_valid = true"

docs.title: Inheritance Rules
docs.text:
Level Priority Table-level filter Highest (overrides suite default) Suite-level default Applied if no table-level filter No filter All data processed

Note: Table-level filters completely replace suite defaults (no merging).

docs.title: Filter Check Output
docs.text:
When filters are applied, a data_filter check is automatically added to results. Its details field is a short status string:

check_name: data_filter
passed: true
details: status=ok

The before/after row counts are not in details; they are recorded in the check's execution.filters_applied trace (rows_before, rows_after), alongside the rest of the execution trace.

docs.title: Empty Result Handling
docs.text:
If filtering results in zero rows:

check_name: data_filter
passed: true
severity: warning
details: status=no_rows_after_filter

The check passes with a warning, and no further checks are executed for that table.

docs.title: Example 1: Production Daily Validation
docs.text:
Validate only today's data across all tables:

silver:
  defaults:
    partition_filter:
      auto: true  # Latest partition for all tables

  tables:
    - catalog: prod_catalog
      schema: sales
      table: orders
      checks:
        idempotency:
          enabled: true
          severity: critical
          blocking: true
          key_columns: [order_id]

    - catalog: prod_catalog
      schema: sales
      table: payments
      checks:
        referential_integrity:
          enabled: true
          source_schema: sales
          source_table: payments
          source_column: order_id
          target:
            schema: sales
            table: orders
            column: order_id

docs.title: Example 2: Rolling Window Validation
docs.text:
Validate last 7 days of data:

gold:
  defaults:
    partition_filter:
      auto_latest: 7

  tables:
    - catalog: analytics
      schema: metrics
      table: daily_revenue
      checks:
        volume:
          enabled: true
          metric: "SUM(revenue)"
          min_value: 1

docs.title: Example 3: Segment-Specific Validation
docs.text:
Validate only completed orders in a specific region:

silver:
  tables:
    - catalog: prod_catalog
      schema: sales
      table: orders
      partition_filter:
        region: "EU"
        date: ["2024-01-14", "2024-01-15"]
      row_filter: "status = 'COMPLETED' AND amount > 0"
      checks:
        business_rules:
          enabled: true
          name: valid_completed_orders
          predicate: "shipping_date IS NOT NULL"

docs.title: Example 4: Mixed Filtering Strategies
docs.text:
Different filters for different tables:

bronze:
  defaults:
    partition_filter:
      auto: true  # Default: latest partition

  tables:
    # Uses default (latest partition)
    - catalog: raw
      schema: events
      table: clicks

    # Override: specific date range
    - catalog: raw
      schema: events
      table: purchases
      partition_filter:
        date: ["2024-01-01", "2024-01-02", "2024-01-03"]

    # Override: no partition filter, row filter only
    - catalog: raw
      schema: events
      table: errors
      partition_filter: null  # Disable partition filter
      row_filter: "error_code IS NOT NULL"

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
1. Always use partition filters for large tables - Partition pruning significantly reduces scan time
  2. Prefer auto: true for daily validation - Automatically adapts to data
  3. Use auto_latest: N for trend validation - Rolling window without manual updates

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
1. Set suite-level defaults - Reduces repetition and ensures consistency
  2. Override only when needed - Table-level overrides for exceptions
  3. Document complex filters - Add comments explaining business logic

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
1. Check filter results - Review data_filter check details
  2. Monitor filter_ratio - Unexpected ratios may indicate issues
  3. Handle empty results - Decide if empty filtered data is acceptable

docs.title: Filter Not Applied
docs.text:
Symptom: partition_filter=none in output

Causes: - Table has no partition columns (for auto mode) - No partition values found - Filter configuration error

Solution: Check table metadata and filter syntax

docs.title: Non-Partition Column Warning
docs.text:
Symptom: warning=non_partition_columns=[col1] in output

Cause: Using a non-partition column in partition_filter

Solution: Move non-partition columns to row_filter for better performance

docs.title: Empty Results
docs.text:
Symptom: status=no_rows_after_filter

Causes: - Filter too restrictive - No data for specified partition - Data not yet available

Solution: Verify filter values match actual data
