docs.title: Database Setup
docs.text: The Neco DQ Framework requires a metadata table to persist execution results.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
The history table is used by the framework for:

  • Historical tracking of Data Quality test executions
  • Alerting and auditability
  • Troubleshooting and trend analysis

This section explains how to create the required metadata table and which parts are customizable by each team.

docs.title: Customization Principles
docs.text:
The framework follows a flexible but contract-based approach:

Component Customizable Notes Schema name yes Each team can use their own catalog/database Table names yes Align with team naming conventions Column names no Fixed by framework contract Column types no Fixed by framework contract Column semantics no Fixed by framework contract

This ensures: - Each team can align with its own catalog/database conventions - The framework can reliably write and read metadata without additional configuration

docs.title: DQ Test History Table
docs.text:
Purpose: Stores the outcome of every Data Quality test execution.

Recommendation: Required

This table provides a complete audit trail of all executed checks (passed and failed), enabling: - Historical analysis - Trend monitoring - Debugging and investigation - Compliance and auditability - Alert generation (via alert_description column)

docs.title: Reference SQL Script
docs.text:
Below is a reference implementation used by the framework. It can be reused as-is or adapted only in terms of schema and table names.

-- =========================================================
-- 1. CREATE SCHEMA
-- =========================================================
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS my_dq_catalog.dq_metadata;

-- =========================================================
-- 2. CREATE TABLE: dq_test_history
-- Stores all DQ check results
-- =========================================================
CREATE TABLE my_dq_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history (
    run_timestamp TIMESTAMP,
    test_suite STRING,
    catalog STRING,
    schema STRING,
    table STRING,
    column STRING,
    passed BOOLEAN,
    status STRING,
    check_name STRING,
    severity STRING,
    details STRING,
    blocking BOOLEAN,
    alert_description STRING,           -- DEPRECATED: use details + check_name instead
    -- v1.1.0 debug experience columns
    execution STRING,
    failure_stats STRING,
    investigation_query STRING
)
USING DELTA;

docs.title: dq_test_history Table
docs.text: Column Type Description run_timestamp TIMESTAMP When the check was executed test_suite STRING Suite name (bronze, silver, gold, great_expectations) catalog STRING Catalog of the validated table schema STRING Schema of the validated table table STRING Name of the validated table column STRING Column name (if check is column-specific) passed BOOLEAN Whether the check passed (true) or failed (false) status STRING Status of the check (PASSED, FAILED, WARNING) check_name STRING Name of the executed check severity STRING Severity level (critical, warning) details STRING Human-readable result message blocking BOOLEAN Whether the check is blocking the pipeline alert_description STRING DEPRECATED - Use details + check_name instead execution STRING JSON with performance context (duration_ms, rows_scanned) - v1.1.0+ failure_stats STRING JSON with failure statistics (counts, distributions) - v1.1.0+, only on FAIL investigation_query STRING SQL template for debugging failures - v1.1.0+, only on FAIL

docs.title: Optional: Separate Alerts Table
docs.text:
If you need a dedicated table for alerts only (e.g., for integration with alerting systems or lightweight monitoring), you can configure a separate destination with alerts: true in your suite's data_to_save configuration.

# In suite.yaml (e.g., suites/bronze/suite.yaml)
data_to_save:
  # History table - all results
  - table: my_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history
    write_mode: append
    alerts: false

  # Alerts table - failed checks only (optional)
  - table: my_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_alerts
    write_mode: append
    alerts: true

The alerts destination (with alerts: true) receives only failed checks, making it useful for: - Integration with alerting systems (PagerDuty, Slack workflows, etc.) - Incident tracking dashboards - Lightweight monitoring without querying full history

docs.title: Per-destination options
docs.text:
Each entry under data_to_save accepts:

Option Type Default Effect table str required Full 3-part destination table (catalog.schema.table) write_mode str append How to write (append) alerts bool false When true, write only failed checks (the alerts destination) columns_to_save list[str] all columns Restrict the written columns to this subset, in this order merge_schema bool false Enable Delta schema merge when the result columns evolve 
data_to_save:
  - table: my_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history
    write_mode: append
    alerts: false
    merge_schema: true
    columns_to_save:
      - test_suite
      - catalog
      - schema
      - table
      - column
      - run_timestamp
      - passed
      - status
      - check_name
      - severity
      - details
      - blocking
      - failure_stats       
      - investigation_query  
      - execution

docs.title: What Can Be Changed
docs.text:
Teams may freely change:

Catalog name 

-- Example: Use your team's catalog
my_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history

Schema name 

-- Example: Use your team's schema
my_dq_catalog.my_team_dq.dq_test_history

Table names 

-- Example: Use your team's naming convention
my_dq_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_execution_history

Configuration:

After creating tables with custom names, update your suite's data_to_save configuration:

# In suite.yaml (e.g., suites/bronze/suite.yaml)
data_to_save:
  - table: my_catalog.my_schema.my_history_table
    write_mode: append
    alerts: false

docs.title: What Must Remain Unchanged
docs.text:
The following must not be modified:

Column names 

-- WRONG: Renaming columns
CREATE TABLE ... (
    execution_time TIMESTAMP,  -- should be run_timestamp
    suite STRING,               -- should be test_suite
    ...
)

Column data types 

-- WRONG: Changing data types
CREATE TABLE ... (
    run_timestamp STRING,       -- should be TIMESTAMP
    passed INT,                 -- should be BOOLEAN
    ...
)

Why this matters:

The framework relies on this schema contract to: - Normalize results across test suites - Generate summaries and alerts - Support future integrations (e.g., dashboards, Allure, BI tools) - Enable cross-team consistency

docs.title: Example: Custom Setup
docs.text:
Here's an example of a customized setup for a team:

-- Team-specific catalog and schema
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS data_analytics_prod.quality_checks;

-- Custom table name following team conventions
CREATE TABLE data_analytics_prod.quality_checks.validation_history (
    run_timestamp TIMESTAMP,
    test_suite STRING,
    catalog STRING,
    schema STRING,
    table STRING,
    column STRING,
    passed BOOLEAN,
    status STRING,
    check_name STRING,
    severity STRING,
    details STRING,
    blocking BOOLEAN,
    alert_description STRING,           -- DEPRECATED: use details + check_name instead
    -- v1.1.0 debug experience columns
    execution STRING,
    failure_stats STRING,
    investigation_query STRING
)
USING DELTA;

Configuration:

# In suite.yaml
data_to_save:
  - table: data_analytics_prod.quality_checks.validation_history
    write_mode: append
    alerts: false

docs.title: Delta Tables
docs.text: Tables are created as Delta tables for: - ACID transactions - Time travel capabilities - Efficient updates and deletes - Schema evolution support

docs.title: Partitioning
docs.text:
Default: No partitioning is enforced

Optional: Teams may add partitioning later if needed:

CREATE TABLE my_dq_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history (
    run_timestamp TIMESTAMP,
    test_suite STRING,
    catalog STRING,
    schema STRING,
    table STRING,
    column STRING,
    passed BOOLEAN,
    status STRING,
    check_name STRING,
    severity STRING,
    details STRING,
    blocking BOOLEAN,
    alert_description STRING,           -- DEPRECATED: use details + check_name instead
    -- v1.1.0 debug experience columns
    execution STRING,
    failure_stats STRING,
    investigation_query STRING
)
USING DELTA
PARTITIONED BY (DATE(run_timestamp), test_suite);

docs.title: Retention and Cleanup
docs.text:
Responsibility: Owning team

Recommendation: Implement retention policies based on your needs:

-- Example: Delete history older than 90 days
DELETE FROM my_dq_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history
WHERE run_timestamp < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL 90 DAYS;

-- Example: Vacuum to reclaim space
VACUUM my_dq_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history RETAIN 168 HOURS;

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Ensure the framework has appropriate permissions:

-- Grant write permissions to the service account
GRANT INSERT, SELECT ON TABLE my_dq_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history
  TO `service_account@example.com`;

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
After creating the table, verify it is accessible:

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()

# Verify history table
history_df = spark.sql("""
    SELECT * FROM my_dq_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history
    LIMIT 1
""")
print("History table accessible: OK")

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Aspect Flexibility Catalog/Schema yes, customizable Table names yes, customizable Column contract no, fixed by framework Partitioning yes, team decision Retention yes, team responsibility

Key Takeaways:

  1. The framework does not enforce a central schema
  2. The framework does enforce a strict metadata contract
  3. The provided SQL is a reference implementation, not a hard dependency
  4. This approach enables gradual adoption across teams without changing the overall Data Quality policy model

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
After setting up the metadata table:

  1. Configure persistence in your YAML files
  2. Run a test validation to verify writes work
  3. Query the history table to see results
  4. Set up retention policies for long-term maintenance

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Getting Started - Complete tutorial
  • Modular Config - Configure the framework

docs.title: Modular Configuration
docs.text: Modular configuration is the recommended approach for production use. It organizes validations into a directory structure that's organized, scalable, and version-control friendly.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Modular configuration separates concerns into focused files: - Global settings: Shared policy, alerts, metadata - Suite directories: One per validation layer (bronze, silver, gold) - Test groups: Logical groupings of related tests - Great Expectations: GE-specific configurations

docs.title: Directory Structure
docs.text:
The root folder name is up to your team (config/, dq-config/, quality-checks/, etc.). The framework only requires the internal structure: global/ and suites/ directories.

config/                          # Any name you choose
├── global/
│   ├── policy.yaml              # Failure handling policy
└── suites/
    ├── bronze/
    │   ├── suite.yaml       # Bronze suite configuration
    │   ├── test_groups/
    │   │   ├── schema.yaml
    │   │   ├── nulls.yaml
    │   │   ├── primary_keys.yaml
    │   │   └── completeness.yaml
    │   └── great_expectations/
    │       └── expectations.json
    ├── silver/
    │   ├── suite.yaml
    │   ├── test_groups/
    │   │   ├── transformations.yaml
    │   │   ├── business_rules.yaml
    │   │   └── data_quality.yaml
    │   └── great_expectations/
    │       └── expectations.json
    └── gold/
        ├── suite.yaml
        ├── test_groups/
        │   ├── aggregations.yaml
        │   ├── metrics.yaml
        │   └── completeness.yaml
        └── great_expectations/
            └── expectations.json

docs.title: global/policy.yaml
docs.text:
Defines failure handling behavior:

dq_policy:
  # Optional: Informational threshold (0.0 to 1.0)
  # Shown in summary when exceeded, but doesn't change pass/fail behavior by default
  failure_threshold: 0.1

  # Optional: When true, non-blocking failures exceeding threshold cause FAIL instead of WARN
  block_on_threshold: false

  # Control which test suites can block the pipeline
  block_test_suites:
    profiling: false
    bronze: true
    silver: true
    gold: true
    great_expectations: true

  alerts:
    slack:
      enabled: true

Policy Options:

Option Type Default Description failure_threshold float None Informational threshold (0.0-1.0). Shown in summary when exceeded. block_on_threshold bool false When true, non-blocking failures exceeding threshold cause FAIL instead of WARN. block_test_suites.<suite> bool true Whether blocking failures in this suite cause pipeline to fail.

Exit Code Behavior:

  • Blocking failures: Always cause FAIL (exit code 20) regardless of threshold
  • Non-blocking failures: Cause WARN (exit code 10) by default
  • block_on_threshold: true: Non-blocking failures exceeding threshold escalate to FAIL

docs.title: Suite Configuration
docs.text: Each suite has its own directory under suites/.

docs.title: suites/bronze/suite.yaml
docs.text:
Bronze suite configuration:

suite: bronze

default_checks:
  record_count:
    enabled: true
    severity: critical
    blocking: true

  table_freshness:
    enabled: true
    severity: warning
    blocking: false

data_to_save:
  - table: my_dq_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history
    write_mode: append
    alerts: false
    columns_to_save:
      - test_suite
      - catalog
      - schema
      - table
      - column
      - run_timestamp
      - passed
      - status
      - check_name
      - severity
      - details
      - blocking

docs.title: Test Groups
docs.text: Test groups organize related validations into separate files for better organization.

docs.title: suites/bronze/test_groups/raw_events.yaml
docs.text:
tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema_bronze
      table: raw_events

      checks:
        freshness:
          enabled: true
          timestamp_column: batch_raw_events_at
          max_delay_hours: 24

        schema_drift:
          enabled: true
          expected_columns:
            batch_raw_events_at: timestamp
            created_at: string
            updated_at: string
            item_created_at: string
            completed_at: string
            batch_id: string
            project_id: string
            order_id: string
            channel_id: string
            owner_group: string
            owner_id: string
            owner_email: string
            transaction_id: string
            customer_id: string
            customer_email: string
            is_duplicate: string
            channel_type: string
            status: string
            template_id: string
            content: string
            event_data: string

        mandatory_fields:
          enabled: true
          columns:
            - batch_raw_events_at
            - batch_id
            - project_id
            - order_id
            - transaction_id

        record_count_anomaly:
          enabled: true
          history_table: my_dq_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history
          max_deviation_percent: 40

docs.title: How Test Groups Work
docs.text:
Test groups are automatically merged into the suite configuration:

suite.yaml
    ↓
ConfigResolver reads
    ↓
Merges test_groups/*.yaml
    ↓
Produces unified config
    ↓
Passed to suite

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
Organized: Related tests grouped logically

Reusable: Test groups can be shared across suites

Maintainable: Easier to find and update tests

Collaborative: Team members can work on different groups

docs.title: Default Checks Inheritance
docs.text: The default_checks section in suite.yaml defines checks that are automatically applied to all tables in that suite. It's how you keep validation consistent across your data without repeating checks per table.

docs.title: How Inheritance Works
docs.text:
suite.yaml (default_checks)
         │
         ▼
┌────────────────────────┐
│  All tables inherit    │
│  default_checks        │
└────────────────────────┘
         │
         ▼
┌────────────────────────┐
│  Table-specific checks │
│  can OVERRIDE or ADD   │
└────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Example: suite.yaml with default_checks
docs.text:
# suites/bronze/suite.yaml
suite: bronze

default_checks:
  # These checks apply to ALL tables in this suite
  record_count:
    enabled: true
    severity: warning
    blocking: false

  table_freshness:
    enabled: true
    severity: warning
    blocking: false
    max_staleness_days: 2

  mandatory_fields:
    enabled: true
    severity: critical
    blocking: true
    columns:
      - batch_id
      - created_at

docs.title: Example: Table inheriting and overriding
docs.text:
# suites/bronze/test_groups/orders.yaml
tables:
  - catalog: my_catalog
    schema: my_schema
    table: orders

    checks:
      # This OVERRIDES the default mandatory_fields with different columns
      mandatory_fields:
        enabled: true
        severity: critical
        blocking: true
        columns:
          - order_id
          - customer_id
          - order_date

      # This ADDS a new check specific to this table
      freshness:
        enabled: true
        timestamp_column: order_date
        max_delay_hours: 24

      # record_count and table_freshness are INHERITED automatically

Result: The orders table will have:

Check Source record_count Inherited from default_checks table_freshness Inherited from default_checks mandatory_fields Overridden with table-specific columns freshness Added specifically for this table

docs.title: Disabling an Inherited Check
docs.text:
To disable a default check for a specific table:

tables:
  - catalog: my_catalog
    schema: my_schema
    table: legacy_table

    checks:
      # Disable the inherited record_count check
      record_count:
        enabled: false

docs.title: Running DQ checks
docs.text:
Once the config tree is in place, run it with run_dq():

from neco_dq.runner import run_dq

# Run all suites in the config directory
results = run_dq("/Workspace/config/")

run_dq() also takes run_suites / exclude_suites, a runtime selector to pick tables, tags, profile and verbose. The full parameter table, the filtering model and end-to-end examples live on the run_dq() API Reference.

docs.title: Multi-environment (profiles)
docs.text: Profiles let one config target dev / staging / prod without duplicating files, via Jinja2 templates ({{ profile.target_catalog }}, {{ var.* }}) resolved at load time. Add a profiles.yml to the config directory and pass profile="prod" (or set NECO_DQ_PROFILE). See Multi-Environment (Profiles) for the full setup.

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text: Here's a complete modular configuration for a production project:

docs.title: Directory Structure
docs.text:
/Workspace/config/sales_dq/
├── global/
│   └── policy.yaml
└── suites/
    ├── bronze/
    │   ├── suite.yaml              # Default checks for all bronze tables
    │   ├── test_groups/
    │   │   ├── raw_events.yaml      # Ingestion layer tables
    │   │   ├── events.yaml         # Event tables
    │   │   └── metadata.yaml       # Metadata tables
    │   └── great_expectations/
    │       └── column_checks.yaml
    ├── silver/
    │   ├── suite.yaml              # Default checks for all silver tables
    │   ├── test_groups/

tables:
  # This table uses default idempotency (with id column) and freshness
  - catalog: my_catalog
    schema: silver
    table: customers
    checks:
      # Add table-specific check
      mandatory_fields:
        enabled: true
        columns: [customer_id, email, created_at]

  # This table overrides the default idempotency key
  - catalog: my_catalog
    schema: silver
    table: orders
    checks:
      # Override: use order_id instead of id
      idempotency:
        enabled: true
        severity: critical
        blocking: true
        key_columns: [order_id]

      # Add referential integrity check
      referential_integrity:
        enabled: true
        source_schema: silver
        source_table: orders
        source_column: customer_id
        target:
          schema: silver
          table: customers
          column: customer_id

# Full validation

# Quick validation: only silver core entities
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/sales_dq/",
    run_suites=["silver"],
    selector={"silver": ["customers", "orders"]}
)

docs.title: Parameter Naming Conventions
docs.text:
Every check reads its settings from a YAML block. Across ~35 checks and three suites, those settings follow a small set of naming conventions so that a key means the same thing wherever it appears. This page is the reference for those conventions, for the deprecated keys that were renamed to follow them, and for how the framework treats unknown keys.

Scope

These conventions describe check parameter keys: the settings inside a check block (timestamp_column, tolerance_abs, …). They do not change the threshold block, which is documented in Thresholds, nor the suite/table structure (catalog, schema, table) of a config file.

docs.title: The conventions
docs.text:
1. Columns end in _column or _columns, with a role prefix when there is more than one. One column is <role>_column (e.g. timestamp_column, status_column, source_column); a list is <role>_columns (e.g. key_columns, join_columns, gold_join_columns).

  2. Numeric limits use min_ / max_ with a noun. A bound is never a bare min / max; it names what it bounds: min_count, min_value, max_value, min_distinct_count, max_distinct_count, min_bytes, max_bytes.

  3. Percentages use _percent and are expressed on a 0–100 scale. Keys such as tolerance_percent, max_deviation_percent, max_parse_failure_percent, min_valid_percent all take 5.0 to mean "5%". A genuine 0–1 fraction keeps the _ratio suffix instead; the suffix tells you the scale.

  4. Tolerance is always qualified. A bare tolerance is forbidden because its unit is ambiguous. Use tolerance_abs for an absolute difference in the metric's own units, or tolerance_percent for a relative deviation (0–100).

  5. Time-unit limits are max_<quantity>_<unit>. The unit is part of the key, so there is no ambiguity about seconds vs hours vs days: max_delay_hours, max_staleness_days.

  6. Referenced tables use a nested block with a role prefix. A table other than the one under validation is given as a nested {catalog, schema, table, column?} block (e.g. the gold referential_integrity silver: block), or as role-prefixed flat keys (source_schema, detail_table, right_schema).

  7. Role prefixes are directional or symmetric. Directional comparisons use source_ / target_ or gold_ / silver_ (the data flows one way). Symmetric comparisons use left_ / right_ (neither side is privileged).

  8. Filters are <role>_filter; a row assertion is predicate. Row-scoping SQL is source_filter, target_filter, left_filter, right_filter. The boolean expression a row must satisfy (in business_rules) is predicate.

  9. Aggregate expressions are <role>_expr. The SQL evaluated on each side of a comparison is gold_expr, silver_expr, left_expr, right_expr.

  10. Collections are expected_* / allowed_*. Sets the data is checked against are named for their role: expected_values, expected_columns, allowed_values, allowed_fingerprints, allowed_flow.

  11. The current table is implicit. The table a check runs on comes from its place in the config (its table_ctx); you do not re-declare it. Keys that could point back at it (left_table, source_schema, …) are therefore optional and default to the current table; supply them only to point at a different table. For the same reason, keys that would redefine the current table as the "other" side are forbidden (e.g. target_* on flow_completeness, whose implicit target is the current table).

docs.title: Deprecated keys and their canonical names
docs.text: Keys that pre-dated these conventions still work: the framework accepts the old name, rewrites it to the canonical one, and records a deprecation. The old names are listed here so existing configs can be migrated.

docs.title: Shared checks (Bronze / Silver / Gold)
docs.text: Check Deprecated key Canonical key distinct_count min, max min_distinct_count, max_distinct_count freshness column timestamp_column business_rules check predicate json_schema max_parse_failure_pct max_parse_failure_percent compare_metric tolerance tolerance_abs

docs.title: Bronze
docs.text: Check Deprecated key Canonical key record_count_anomaly allowed_deviation_percent max_deviation_percent table_freshness max_days_stale max_staleness_days

docs.title: Silver
docs.text: Check Deprecated key Canonical key idempotency, status_transition key_column key_columns cardinality min min_count totals_consistency join_key, catalog, tolerance join_columns, detail_catalog, tolerance_abs cross_table_equality join_key, tolerance join_columns, tolerance_abs temporal_consistency, row_temporal_consistency join_key, left_timestamp, right_timestamp join_columns, left_timestamp_column, right_timestamp_column flow_completeness join_key, tolerance_pct, lateness.column join_columns, tolerance_percent, lateness.timestamp_column referential_integrity catalog, schema, table, target_catalog / target_schema / target_table / target_column, min_valid_ratio source_catalog, source_schema, source_table, target: {catalog, schema, table, column}, min_valid_percent (0–100)

docs.title: Gold
docs.text:
Check Deprecated key Canonical key reconciliation_expr gold, silver (expression), tolerance, source_silver, filter: {gold, silver}, join_filter: {gold_column, silver_column} gold_expr, silver_expr, tolerance_percent, silver: {catalog, schema, table}, gold_filter / silver_filter, gold_join_columns / silver_join_columns coverage tolerance_pct, join_keys, gold_join_keys, silver_join_keys, silver_table tolerance_percent, join_columns, gold_join_columns, silver_join_columns, silver: {catalog, schema, table} volume min, max, history.tolerance_pct min_value, max_value, history.tolerance_percent cross_gold tolerance tolerance_abs trend history_table, window, min_history, tolerance_pct history: {table, window, min_history, tolerance_percent}

Shape changes beyond renaming

A few parameters changed shape, not just name; their migration is handled automatically but is more than a key swap. The gold coverage silver_table string becomes a nested silver: {catalog, schema, table} block, and the silver referential_integrity target_* keys collapse into a nested target block while min_valid_ratio (0–1) becomes min_valid_percent (0–100). The per-check pages under Test Suites & Checks show the current shape.

docs.title: Deprecation timeline
docs.text:
Release Behaviour of deprecated keys This release New keys are canonical. Old keys are still accepted and silently rewritten, but each one is reported (once per deprecated key, with the number of tables it was seen on) in the verbose run summary and in the programmatic deprecations output. Next major Aliases are removed. Legacy keys are no longer understood and are treated as unknown parameters (see below).

Migrate on your own schedule before the next major: switch each config to the canonical keys and confirm the deprecation report comes back empty.

Check IDs of multi-instance checks

When a check has several instances, each result gets an ID built from the config as written, e.g. idempotency[key_column=id]. Upgrading without touching the config keeps the IDs you already have in history and dashboards. Renaming a key during migration (key_column → key_columns) changes the ID to idempotency[key_columns=id], so history for that instance starts over under the new name.

docs.title: Unknown parameters
docs.text:
Once aliases are resolved, any remaining key a check does not understand is an unknown parameter: usually a typo (kye_columns) or a leftover key. How the framework reacts is controlled per run by the failure policy:

dq_policy:
  unknown_check_params: warn   # warn (default) | error | ignore
Mode Effect warn (default) Log a warning naming the unknown key (and suggesting the closest valid key, e.g. did you mean 'key_columns'?); the key is left in the config and the check still runs. error Raise a CheckConfigError (a ValueError) and fail the whole run, even if other suites succeeded; useful in CI to catch typos before they ship. ignore Accept unknown keys silently: no warning, no error.

An invalid value for unknown_check_params falls back to warn. Checks that are not described in the parameter schema are skipped by this validation, so a custom or newly added check never produces false warnings.

The same policy governs forbidden keys (keys that are structurally disallowed for a check, such as target_* on flow_completeness): warn logs that the key is not allowed, error fails the run, ignore says nothing.

docs.title: Failure Policy
docs.text:
The policy engine decides the final outcome of a run: it looks at every check result and returns a single exit code. It runs strictly after all suites have executed, never during, so suites only produce results and the policy alone decides consequences.

Policy is configured under dq_policy (in global/policy.yaml for modular configs, or at the top level of a single-file config).

docs.title: The four knobs, and how they interact
docs.text:
Four separate settings decide whether a failing check fails the pipeline or only warns. They are easy to confuse, so here is what each one actually does:

Setting Where Default Effect blocking per check false If a check with blocking: true fails, the run fails (exit 20). A failing non-blocking check only warns. severity per check warning Label (critical / error / warning / info) shown in the summary. It does not by itself decide the exit code, it describes the check. block_test_suites.<suite> per suite (policy) true Whether a suite is allowed to block at all. Set a suite to false and its blocking failures are downgraded to warnings. block_on_threshold + failure_threshold global (policy) false / none If enabled, a global failure rate above the threshold escalates warnings to a failure.

blocking defaults to false

Every check is non-blocking unless you set blocking: true. There is no suite that makes its checks blocking automatically, not Silver, not Gold. The common convention is to set correctness checks (Silver/Gold) to blocking: true and leave Bronze ingestion checks as warnings, but that is your choice in config, not a framework default.

docs.title: How the exit code is decided
docs.text:
The engine evaluates results in this order (see dq_failure_policy.py):

  1. Any blocking failure in a suite that is allowed to block → FAIL (exit 20). This wins over everything else.
  2. Otherwise, any non-blocking failure with severity warning, error or critical → WARN (exit 10). Failures whose only severity is info do not raise a warning. If block_on_threshold: true and the global failure rate exceeds failure_threshold, this escalates to FAIL (exit 20) instead.
  3. Otherwise → SUCCESS (exit 0).

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Exit code Status Meaning 0 SUCCESS All checks passed 10 WARN Failures occurred, none blocking 20 FAIL At least one blocking failure (or threshold escalation) 99 SYSTEM_ERROR Invalid configuration or a malformed summary

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
dq_policy:
  # Optional: informational failure-rate threshold (0.0 to 1.0).
  # Shown in the summary when exceeded. On its own it does not change pass/fail.
  failure_threshold: 0.1

  # Optional: when true, a global failure rate above failure_threshold
  # turns WARN into FAIL.
  block_on_threshold: false

  # Which suites are allowed to block the pipeline.
  block_test_suites:
    profiling: false
    bronze: true
    silver: true
    gold: true
    great_expectations: true

  alerts:
    slack:
      enabled: true

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Description failure_threshold float none Informational threshold (0.0 to 1.0), shown in the summary when the global failure rate exceeds it. block_on_threshold bool false When true, a global failure rate above failure_threshold escalates WARN to FAIL. block_test_suites.<suite> bool true Whether blocking failures in that suite fail the pipeline. Set to false to make a suite warning-only. alerts.slack.enabled bool false Send a Slack summary. See Slack Alerts.

Threshold is measured globally

failure_threshold compares total failed checks against total checks across all suites, not per suite.

docs.title: Per-environment overrides
docs.text: Policy values can differ per environment through profiles, so dev can be warning-only while prod blocks. See Policy Overrides.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text: Adapt one data quality configuration to multiple environments (dev, staging, prod) without duplicating files.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Profiles allow you to maintain a single configuration structure that adapts to different environments (dev, staging, prod) without duplicating files. Each profile defines environment-specific values that are injected into your YAML configuration via Jinja2 templates.

docs.title: When to Use Profiles
docs.text: Use Case Example Multi-environment deployments Same config for dev/staging/prod with different catalogs Team-specific configs Different thresholds for different teams Feature flags Enable/disable checks per environment Parameterized validation Different SLAs per environment

docs.title: 1. Create profiles.yml
docs.text:
Place this file in your config directory (alongside your YAML config or at the root of your modular config).

default_profile: dev

profiles:
  dev:
    target_catalog: dev_catalog
    variables:
      schema_prefix: dev_
      max_delay_hours: 48
      failure_threshold: 0.2

  prod:
    target_catalog: prod_catalog
    variables:
      schema_prefix: ""
      max_delay_hours: 24
      failure_threshold: 0.05

docs.title: 2. Use Variables in Config
docs.text:
Reference profile values using Jinja2 syntax:

bronze:
  tables:
    - catalog: "{{ profile.target_catalog }}"
      schema: "{{ var.schema_prefix }}my_schema"
      table: my_table
      checks:
        freshness:
          enabled: true
          max_delay_hours: "{{ var.max_delay_hours }}"

docs.title: 3. Run with Profile
docs.text:
from neco_dq.runner import run_dq

# Explicit profile parameter
results = run_dq("/Workspace/config/", profile="prod")

# Or use environment variable
# export NECO_DQ_PROFILE=prod
results = run_dq("/Workspace/config/")

docs.title: Profile Resolution Order
docs.text:
The framework resolves the active profile in this order (highest priority first):

Priority Source Example 1 profile parameter in run_dq() run_dq(..., profile="prod") 2 NECO_DQ_PROFILE environment variable export NECO_DQ_PROFILE=prod 3 default_profile in profiles.yml default_profile: dev 4 Fallback to "default" If no profile specified and no default_profile set

docs.title: profiles.yml Structure
docs.text:
Profile names and variable names are completely up to your team. Use whatever naming convention makes sense for your organization.

# Optional: set the default profile when none is specified
default_profile: dev

profiles:
  # Profile names are free-form: dev, prod, staging, team_a, daily_run, etc.
  dev:
    # Accessible as {{ profile.target_catalog }}
    target_catalog: dev_catalog

    # Variable names are free-form: use whatever your team prefers
    # Accessible as {{ var.name }}
    variables:
      schema_prefix: dev_
      max_delay_hours: 48
      enable_expensive_checks: false

    # Optional: override dq_policy settings for this profile
    policy:
      failure_threshold: 0.2
      block_test_suites:
        bronze: false

  staging:
    target_catalog: staging_catalog
    variables:
      schema_prefix: stg_
      max_delay_hours: 36
      enable_expensive_checks: true

  prod:
    target_catalog: prod_catalog
    variables:
      schema_prefix: ""
      max_delay_hours: 24
      enable_expensive_checks: true
    policy:
      failure_threshold: 0.05

docs.title: Profile Fields
docs.text:
Field Type Description target_catalog str Default catalog, accessible as {{ profile.target_catalog }} variables dict User-defined variables, accessible as {{ var.name }} policy dict Policy overrides merged with global dq_policy

Naming is flexible: Profile names (dev, prod, team_analytics, nightly_run) and variable names (max_delay_hours, target_schema, enable_feature_x) are entirely up to your team. The framework imposes no naming conventions.

docs.title: Profile Inheritance
docs.text:
Profiles can extend other profiles using the extends keyword. Child profiles inherit all values from the parent, with child values taking precedence.

profiles:
  base:
    target_catalog: base_catalog
    variables:
      max_delay_hours: 24
      enable_alerts: true
      alert_channel: "#dq-alerts"

  dev:
    extends: base
    target_catalog: dev_catalog  # Override
    variables:
      max_delay_hours: 48        # Override
      # enable_alerts and alert_channel inherited from base

  prod:
    extends: base
    target_catalog: prod_catalog
    variables:
      max_delay_hours: 12        # Stricter than base

docs.title: Inheritance Rules
docs.text:
1. Child values override parent values at the same key
  2. variables dicts are deep-merged (child adds/overrides individual keys)
  3. Other fields are replaced entirely
  4. Circular inheritance is detected and raises an error

docs.title: Available Variables
docs.text: Variable Source Example {{ profile.name }} Active profile name "prod" {{ profile.target_catalog }} Profile's target_catalog "prod_catalog" {{ var.<name> }} Profile's variables.<name> {{ var.freshness_hours }}

docs.title: Type Conversion
docs.text:
Jinja2 templates always produce strings. The framework automatically converts them back to the appropriate types:

Template Value Converted To "123" 123 (int) "12.5" 12.5 (float) "true" / "false" True / False (bool) "[1, 2, 3]" [1, 2, 3] (list)

docs.title: Conditionals
docs.text:
Use Jinja2 conditionals for environment-specific checks:

checks:
  expensive_check:
    enabled: {{ var.enable_expensive_checks }}

{% if var.enable_alerts %}
  alert_channel: "{{ var.alert_channel }}"
{% endif %}

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
Use the default filter for optional variables:

checks:
  freshness:
    max_delay_hours: {{ var.max_delay_hours | default(24) }}

docs.title: Lists and Dicts
docs.text:
Use the tojson filter for complex values:

variables:
  required_columns: ["id", "created_at", "updated_at"]

# In config:
mandatory_fields:
  columns: {{ var.required_columns | tojson }}

docs.title: Policy Overrides
docs.text: Profiles can override dq_policy settings. Profile policy values are merged with global policy, with profile values taking precedence.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
global/policy.yaml: 

dq_policy:
  failure_threshold: 0.1
  block_test_suites:
    bronze: true
    silver: true
    gold: true

profiles.yml: 

profiles:
  dev:
    policy:
      failure_threshold: 0.5      # More lenient in dev
      block_on_threshold: false   # Don't escalate to FAIL
      block_test_suites:
        bronze: false             # Don't block on bronze in dev

  prod:
    policy:
      failure_threshold: 0.05     # Strict in prod
      block_on_threshold: true    # FAIL if threshold exceeded

Result for dev profile: 

dq_policy:
  failure_threshold: 0.5      # From profile
  block_on_threshold: false   # From profile
  block_test_suites:
    bronze: false             # From profile
    silver: true              # From global
    gold: true                # From global

docs.title: Policy Options
docs.text: Option Type Description failure_threshold float Informational threshold (0.0-1.0). Shown in summary when exceeded. block_on_threshold bool When true, non-blocking failures exceeding threshold cause FAIL instead of WARN. block_test_suites.<suite> bool Whether blocking failures in this suite cause pipeline to fail.

docs.title: Threshold Behavior
docs.text:
• Blocking failures: Always cause FAIL regardless of threshold
  • Non-blocking failures: Cause WARN by default
  • block_on_threshold: true: Non-blocking failures exceeding threshold escalate to FAIL
  • Summary displays threshold when configured: Success Rate: 85.7% │ Threshold: 10% │ Status: WARN

docs.title: File Location
docs.text:
The framework searches for profiles.yml (or profiles.yaml) in these locations:

Config Type Search Order Modular config {config_dir}/profiles.yml → {config_dir}/global/profiles.yml Single-file config {parent_dir}/profiles.yml → {parent_dir}/global/profiles.yml

docs.title: Example Directory Structures
docs.text:
Modular config (profiles.yml at root): 

/Workspace/dq-config/
├── profiles.yml              # ← Found first
├── global/
│   └── policy.yaml
└── suites/
    └── bronze/
        └── suite.yaml

Modular config (profiles.yml in global/): 

/Workspace/dq-config/
├── global/
│   ├── profiles.yml          # ← Also valid location
│   └── policy.yaml
└── suites/
    └── bronze/
        └── suite.yaml

Single-file config: 

/Workspace/dq-config/
├── profiles.yml              # ← Found first
└── bronze_suite.yaml

docs.title: Directory Structure
docs.text:
/Workspace/dq-config/
├── profiles.yml
├── global/
│   └── policy.yaml
└── suites/
    └── bronze/
        ├── suite.yaml
        └── test_groups/
            └── ingestion.yaml

docs.title: profiles.yml
docs.text:
default_profile: dev

profiles:
  base:
    variables:
      dq_catalog: dq_metadata_catalog
      dq_schema: dq_metadata
      enable_alerts: true

  dev:
    extends: base
    target_catalog: dev_catalog
    variables:
      schema_prefix: dev_
      max_delay_hours: 72
    policy:
      failure_threshold: 0.5
      block_test_suites:
        bronze: false

  staging:
    extends: base
    target_catalog: staging_catalog
    variables:
      schema_prefix: stg_
      max_delay_hours: 48

  prod:
    extends: base
    target_catalog: prod_catalog
    variables:
      schema_prefix: ""
      max_delay_hours: 24
    policy:
      failure_threshold: 0.05

docs.title: global/policy.yaml
docs.text:
dq_policy:
  failure_threshold: 0.1
  block_test_suites:
    bronze: true
    silver: true
    gold: true
  alerts:
    slack:
      enabled: "{{ var.enable_alerts }}"

docs.title: suites/bronze/suite.yaml
docs.text:
suite: bronze

data_to_save:
  - table: "{{ var.dq_catalog }}.{{ var.dq_schema }}.dq_test_history"
    write_mode: append

docs.title: suites/bronze/test_groups/ingestion.yaml
docs.text:
tables:
  - catalog: "{{ profile.target_catalog }}"
    schema: "{{ var.schema_prefix }}raw_data"
    table: events
    checks:
      freshness:
        enabled: true
        timestamp_column: batch_ingestion_at
        max_delay_hours: "{{ var.max_delay_hours }}"

      record_count:
        enabled: true   # fails only when the table is empty

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
from neco_dq.runner import run_dq

# Development (lenient thresholds, dev catalog)
results = run_dq("/Workspace/dq-config/", profile="dev")

# Production (strict thresholds, prod catalog)
results = run_dq("/Workspace/dq-config/", profile="prod")

# CI/CD pipeline (use environment variable)
# export NECO_DQ_PROFILE=staging
results = run_dq("/Workspace/dq-config/")

docs.title: 1. Use Base Profile for Shared Config
docs.text:
profiles:
  base:
    variables:
      dq_catalog: qa_dq
      common_setting: value

  dev:
    extends: base
    # Only override what differs

  prod:
    extends: base
    # Only override what differs

docs.title: 2. Keep Environment Differences Minimal
docs.text:
Focus profiles on values that truly differ: - Catalog/schema names - Thresholds and SLAs - Feature flags

Avoid duplicating check definitions across profiles.

docs.title: 3. Use Defaults for Optional Variables
docs.text:
max_delay_hours: {{ var.max_delay_hours | default(24) }}

This makes configs work even without profiles.

docs.title: 4. Document Profile-Specific Behavior
docs.text:
Add comments explaining why values differ:

prod:
  variables:
    # Production SLA: data must be fresh within 24 hours
    max_delay_hours: 24

docs.title: 5. Set Sensible Defaults in default_profile
docs.text: default_profile: dev  # Safe default for local development

docs.title: Profile Not Found
docs.text:
ProfileNotFoundError: Unknown profile 'staging'. Available: dev, prod

Solution: Check profile name spelling in profiles.yml.

docs.title: Undefined Variable
docs.text:
jinja2.exceptions.UndefinedError: 'var' is undefined

Solution: Ensure profiles.yml exists and defines the variable, or use | default().

docs.title: Circular Inheritance
docs.text:
CircularInheritanceError: Circular inheritance detected: dev -> staging -> dev

Solution: Review extends chain and remove the cycle.

docs.title: Type Conversion Issues
docs.text:
If a numeric value is being treated as a string, ensure you're not quoting it:

# Wrong - will be string "24"
max_delay_hours: "{{ var.max_delay_hours }}"

# Right - auto-converted to int
max_delay_hours: {{ var.max_delay_hours }}

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Modular Config - Directory-based configuration
  • Single-File Configuration - Single-file configuration
  • Template System - Advanced Jinja2 patterns
  • Data Filtering - Scope validation to subsets

docs.title: Running DQ
docs.text:
run_dq() is the main entry point for executing data quality checks. This page is the reference for its parameters and the filtering model. For how to structure a config, see Modular Configuration.

from neco_dq.runner import run_dq

results = run_dq(
    config_ref,              # Path to config directory or file
    profile=None,            # Optional: profile name from profiles.yml
    run_suites=None,         # Optional: only run these suites
    exclude_suites=None,     # Optional: skip these suites
    selector=None,           # Optional: filter specific tables per suite
    tags=None,               # Optional: only run checks with matching tags
    custom_suite_files=None, # Optional: Python file(s) with custom suites
    verbose=False,           # Optional: show debug output and progress bars
)

run_dq() returns a dict[str, Any]: a summary of results keyed per test suite.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description config_ref str required Path to config directory or YAML file profile str None Profile name from profiles.yml (else NECO_DQ_PROFILE or default_profile) run_suites list[str] None Only run these test suites exclude_suites list[str] None Skip these test suites selector dict[str, list[str]] None Filter specific tables per suite tags list[str] None Only run checks with matching tags custom_suite_files str \| list[str] None Path(s) to Python file(s) with custom DQTestSuite(s). See Custom Suites. verbose bool False Enable debug logging and progress bars

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
from neco_dq.runner import run_dq

# Run all suites in the config directory
results = run_dq("/Workspace/config/")

docs.title: Selective suite execution
docs.text:
Control which test suites to run:

# Run only bronze suite
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    run_suites=["bronze"]
)

# Run bronze and silver suites
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    run_suites=["bronze", "silver"]
)

# Run all suites EXCEPT profiling
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    exclude_suites=["profiling"]
)

# Run gold suite and its Great Expectations checks
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    run_suites=["gold", "great_expectations@gold"]
)

docs.title: Runtime table selection with selector
docs.text: The selector parameter filters which tables to validate at runtime, without modifying your configuration files. This is useful for debugging, incremental validation, or splitting work across parallel jobs.

docs.title: Basic usage
docs.text:
# Run only specific tables in bronze suite
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    run_suites=["bronze"],
    selector={
        "bronze": ["orders", "customers"]  # Only these tables
    }
)

This runs bronze checks only on orders and customers tables, skipping all other tables defined in the configuration.

docs.title: Multiple suites
docs.text:
# Run specific tables in multiple suites
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    run_suites=["bronze", "silver"],
    selector={
        "bronze": ["orders", "customers"],
        "silver": ["orders_cleaned", "customers_enriched"]
    }
)

docs.title: Great Expectations suites
docs.text:
For GE suites, use the parent suite name:

# Config has: great_expectations@silver
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    selector={"silver": ["orders"]}  # Works for both silver and ge@silver
)

selector inheritance for Great Expectations

When you filter tables for a suite, the same filter applies to its Great Expectations checks. For example, selector={"gold": ["summary"]} also filters great_expectations@gold to only run checks on the summary table.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text: Scenario Example Debug single table selector={"bronze": ["problematic_table"]} Incremental validation selector={"silver": ["newly_loaded_table"]} CI/CD subset selector={"gold": ["critical_kpis"]} Parallel jobs Split tables across workers using selector

docs.title: Combining with other filters
docs.text:
selector works with other filtering options:

results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    run_suites=["bronze", "silver"],     # Suite-level filter
    selector={"bronze": ["orders"]},      # Table-level filter
    tags=["critical"]                     # Check-level filter
)

Filter order:

  1. run_suites / exclude_suites: which suites to run
  2. selector: which tables within those suites
  3. tags: which checks within those tables
  4. partition_filter / row_filter: which rows within those tables

See Data Filtering and Tag Filtering for the row- and check-level filters.

docs.title: Verbose mode
docs.text:
Enable detailed logging and progress bars:

results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    verbose=True  # Shows debug output and progress bars
)

docs.title: Running with a profile
docs.text:
# Explicit profile
results = run_dq("/Workspace/config/", profile="prod")

# Or environment variable
# export NECO_DQ_PROFILE=prod
results = run_dq("/Workspace/config/")

See Multi-Environment (Profiles) for the full profile model.

docs.title: Complete example: production usage
docs.text:
from neco_dq.runner import run_dq

# Full validation: all suites, all tables
results = run_dq("/Workspace/config/")

# Quick validation: only bronze, specific tables
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    run_suites=["bronze"],
    selector={"bronze": ["critical_table_1", "critical_table_2"]}
)

# Skip expensive checks: exclude profiling
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    exclude_suites=["profiling"]
)

# Debug mode: verbose output for troubleshooting
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    run_suites=["silver"],
    selector={"silver": ["problem_table"]},
    verbose=True
)

docs.title: Single-File Configuration
docs.text: Single-file configuration mode for simpler projects.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Single-file mode uses one YAML file containing all configuration. It's straightforward for small projects but consider modular configuration as your project grows.

docs.title: When to Use Single-File Mode
docs.text:
Good for: - Quick prototyping and experimentation - Simple projects with 1-2 suites - Learning the framework - Single-table validations - Small teams

Consider modular config when: - Configuration exceeds ~200 lines - Multiple team members edit configs - You want granular version control - You need to reuse test patterns

docs.title: Basic Structure
docs.text:
A single-file config is the same content a modular tree holds, flattened into one YAML: a top-level dq_policy, then one key per suite (bronze, silver, gold, great_expectations), each with tables and checks. Suites also accept default_checks and a data_to_save block. These behave identically to modular mode, so they're documented there rather than repeated here:

  • Policy options → Configuration Basics · policy.yaml
  • default_checks inheritance → Configuration Basics · Default Checks
  • Persistence / data_to_save → Database Setup

A minimal single-file config:

dq_policy:
  block_test_suites:
    bronze: true
  alerts:
    slack:
      enabled: true

bronze:
  default_checks:
    record_count:
      enabled: true
      severity: critical
      blocking: true

  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema_bronze
      table: raw_events
      checks:
        freshness:
          enabled: true
          timestamp_column: batch_raw_events_at
          max_delay_hours: 24

        mandatory_fields:
          enabled: true
          columns: [batch_id, project_id, order_id]

silver:
  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema_silver
      table: cleaned_events
      checks:
        referential_integrity:
          enabled: true
          source_column: order_id
          target:
            schema: my_schema_silver
            table: orders
            column: order_id

Add gold: and great_expectations: keys the same way. Each check's parameters are documented on its suite page (see Test Suites Overview).

docs.title: Loading Configuration
docs.text:
Point run_dq() at the file (not a directory):

from neco_dq.runner import run_dq

results = run_dq("/dbfs/config/dq_config.yaml")

# With a profile for multi-environment support
results = run_dq("/dbfs/config/dq_config.yaml", profile="prod")

See the run_dq() API Reference for all options.

docs.title: 1. Poor Scalability
docs.text:
# As configuration grows, file becomes unmanageable
bronze_suite:
  tables:
    - name: table1  # Line 50
      checks: [...]
    - name: table2  # Line 100
      checks: [...]
    # ... 20 more tables ...
    - name: table22  # Line 1500 - hard to find!

docs.title: 2. Difficult Collaboration
docs.text:
• Merge conflicts on single large file
  • No granular review of changes
  • Hard to track who changed what

docs.title: 3. No Reuse
docs.text:
• Cannot import common validation patterns
  • Must copy-paste repeated validations
  • No test group organization

docs.title: 4. Version Control Issues
docs.text:
• Every change touches one file
  • Difficult to see scope of changes in git diff
  • Cannot track suite evolution separately

docs.title: Using Profiles
docs.text: Profiles work with single-file configs too: put a profiles.yml next to your YAML file, use {{ profile.target_catalog }} / {{ var.* }} templates in the config, and pass profile="prod" (or set NECO_DQ_PROFILE). The mechanics are identical to modular mode, see Multi-Environment (Profiles) for the full setup, inheritance and policy overrides.

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Modular Configuration - Recommended approach
  • Profiles - Multi-environment configuration

docs.title: Slack Alerts
docs.text: Send DQ results to Slack channels.

docs.title: 2. Configure Webhook
docs.text:
Option A: Databricks Secrets (recommended)

databricks secrets create-scope dq-alerts
databricks secrets put-secret dq-alerts slack_webhook_url --string-value "https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ"

These exact names (dq-alerts / slack_webhook_url) are what the framework reads — creating the secret is all that is needed, with no code or task wiring of your own. See Webhook Resolution.

Option B: Environment Variable

export SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL="https://hooks.slack.com/services/XXX/YYY/ZZZ"

For notebooks and local runs only — not reliable on Databricks jobs, and unusable on serverless tasks (see Webhook Resolution). Use the secret there.

docs.title: 3. Enable in Config
docs.text:
dq_policy:
  alerts:
    slack:
      enabled: true

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
dq_policy:
  alerts:
    slack:
      enabled: true
      send_always: false       # Send on PASS/WARN too (default: only FAIL)
      mention_on_fail: false   # Add @channel on FAIL
      include_job_link: true   # Include Databricks job URL
      max_failures_shown: 5    # Max items in Top Failures
      compact_mode: false      # Single-line summary
Option Type Default Description enabled bool false Enable Slack alerts send_always bool false Send on PASS and WARN (not just FAIL) mention_on_fail bool false Add @channel mention on FAIL include_job_link bool true Include Databricks job URL (if available) max_failures_shown int 5 Number of failures shown in Top Failures compact_mode bool false Use single-line compact format

docs.title: Standard Format
docs.text:
*Data Quality Summary*
`prod` • `staging` • 2026-06-12 15:30 UTC

*Status:* *FAIL* (3 blocking)
*Success Rate:* 90.2% (55/61 checks)  •  Threshold: 10%

bronze         🟨    10/11
silver         🟩    15/15
gold           🟥    30/35

*Top Failures:*
• `freshness` → gold.orders (updated_at) (x4)
• `referential_integrity` → gold.orders (customer_id) (x2)

🔗 View Job

The context line shows the active profile and the detected environment. The profile comes from the profile argument; the environment is auto-detected from the Databricks workspace URL. Each is shown only when known, so the line may carry one, both, or neither.

Each Top Failures line pairs a check with the table it actually failed on, followed by the affected columns and the failure count ((x4)).

Elements:

Element When Shown Profile name If profile is set and not "default" Environment If auto-detected from the Databricks workspace (not "unknown") Threshold If failure_threshold is configured Top Failures If there are failures Job link If running on Databricks and include_job_link: true

docs.title: Compact Format
docs.text:
With compact_mode: true:

*DQ FAIL* | `qa` | 2026-06-12 15:30 UTC
Success: *90.2%* (55/61) | *3 blocking*

docs.title: Status Colors
docs.text:
Messages have a colored sidebar based on status:

Status Color Emoji FAIL Red 🟥 WARN Orange 🟨 PASS Green 🟩

docs.title: When Alerts Are Sent
docs.text: Status send_always: false send_always: true FAIL sent sent WARN not sent sent PASS not sent sent

docs.title: Environment Detection
docs.text: The environment shown in the context line is detected from the Databricks workspace URL: a host containing dev, stage/stg, or prod maps to dev, staging, or prod. Outside Databricks, the framework reads the DQ_ENVIRONMENT variable. If neither resolves, the environment is unknown and is omitted from the message.

docs.title: Webhook Resolution
docs.text:
The framework looks for the webhook URL in this order:

  1. Databricks secret (scope: dq-alerts, key: slack_webhook_url)
  2. Environment variable SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL

The scope and key names are fixed — the framework reads exactly dq-alerts / slack_webhook_url and this is not configurable. Create the secret under those names and you are done: the framework resolves it itself at runtime via dbutils, so the webhook never has to pass through your run script, your task parameters, or any wiring of your own. A scope under any other name will not be found.

On Databricks jobs, prefer the secret over the environment variable. A {{secrets/scope/key}} reference does not resolve inside task parameters, and a serverless task has no cluster environment variables in which to set SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL — so the secret is the only path that works there. The environment variable is meant for notebooks and local runs.

The secret lookup is best-effort: if the secret cannot be read — for example the scope exists but the job lacks permission on it — the framework silently falls back to the environment variable and logs the reason only at debug level. So a misconfigured secret looks the same as no secret at all.

If neither is found, alerts are skipped with a warning: 

Slack webhook URL not configured. Skipping alerts.

docs.title: Alerts on Failures Only (Default)
docs.text:
dq_policy:
  alerts:
    slack:
      enabled: true

docs.title: Always Send with @channel on Failure
docs.text:
dq_policy:
  alerts:
    slack:
      enabled: true
      send_always: true
      mention_on_fail: true

docs.title: Compact Mode for High-Frequency Jobs
docs.text:
dq_policy:
  alerts:
    slack:
      enabled: true
      compact_mode: true
      max_failures_shown: 3

docs.title: With Profiles
docs.text:
Different Slack behavior per environment:

# profiles.yml
profiles:
  dev:
    policy:
      alerts:
        slack:
          enabled: false  # No alerts in dev

  prod:
    policy:
      alerts:
        slack:
          enabled: true
          send_always: true
          mention_on_fail: true

docs.title: "Slack webhook URL not configured"
docs.text:
• Check Databricks secret exists: databricks secrets list dq-alerts
  • Confirm the exact names: scope dq-alerts, key slack_webhook_url (both are fixed)
  • Check env var is set: echo $SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL

docs.title: Secret exists but alerts still skip
docs.text: • The job may lack read permission on the dq-alerts scope. The framework falls back to the env var on any read failure and logs the reason only at debug level, so a permission problem is invisible at the default log level. Check the scope ACLs, or raise the log level to see the underlying error.

docs.title: Message Not Appearing
docs.text:
• Verify webhook URL is valid (test with curl)
  • Check enabled: true in config
  • For PASS/WARN, ensure send_always: true

docs.title: No Job Link
docs.text:
• Job link only appears when running as a Databricks job
  • Running in notebook or locally: no job link

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Modular Config - Policy configuration
  • Profiles - Per-environment alert settings

docs.title: Tags Filtering
docs.text:
Tags filtering allows you to selectively run checks based on custom tags. This is useful for:

  • Running only critical checks during time-sensitive operations
  • Separating smoke tests from full validation
  • Scheduling different check groups (hourly, daily, weekly)
  • Isolating expensive checks for off-peak execution

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Tags are configured at the check level and filtered at runtime via the tags parameter.

Key behaviors:

  • Strict filtering: When tags filter is set, checks without tags are skipped
  • OR logic: A check runs if ANY of its tags match ANY filter tag
  • Smart pre-filtering: Only tables with tagged checks are loaded
  • Suite skipping: Suites without any tagged tables are skipped entirely

docs.title: 1. Add Tags to Checks
docs.text:
silver:
  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema
      table: orders
      checks:
        idempotency:
          enabled: true
          severity: critical
          blocking: true
          tags: [critical, daily]
          key_columns: [order_id]

        freshness:
          enabled: true
          severity: warning
          blocking: false
          tags: [daily, smoke]

        record_count:
          enabled: true
          severity: warning
          blocking: false
          tags: [hourly]

docs.title: 2. Run with Tag Filter
docs.text:
from neco_dq.runner import run_dq

# Run only critical checks
results = run_dq("/Workspace/config/", tags=["critical"])

# Run daily checks
results = run_dq("/Workspace/config/", tags=["daily"])

# Run both smoke and critical checks
results = run_dq("/Workspace/config/", tags=["smoke", "critical"])

docs.title: Filtering Behavior
docs.text: Scenario Behavior No tags parameter All checks run (normal behavior) tags set + check has matching tag Check runs tags set + check has non-matching tag Check skipped tags set + check has no tags Check skipped tags set + table has no tagged checks Table not loaded tags set + suite has no tagged tables Suite skipped entirely

docs.title: Bronze / Silver / Gold Suites
docs.text:
Tags are added at the check configuration level:

silver:
  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema
      table: orders
      checks:
        idempotency:
          enabled: true
          severity: critical
          blocking: true
          tags: [critical, daily]
          key_columns: [order_id]

        freshness:
          enabled: true
          severity: warning
          blocking: false
          tags: [daily, smoke]
          timestamp_column: created_at
          max_delay_hours: 24

        record_count:
          enabled: true
          tags: [hourly]
          min_count: 1

        # Check without tags - skipped when filtering
        schema_check:
          enabled: true

docs.title: Great Expectations Suite
docs.text:
For GE, tags are configured at the rule level (inside the column/dataset configuration):

great_expectations:
  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema
      table: orders
      checks:
        order_id:
          not_null:
            enabled: true
            tags: [critical, smoke]   # Tag at rule level
          unique:
            enabled: true
            # No tags = skipped when filtering

        amount:
          between:
            enabled: true
            min: 0
            max: 10000
            tags: [daily]

        _dataset:
          min_rows:
            enabled: true
            value: 1
            tags: [smoke, hourly]

docs.title: List-style Check Configurations
docs.text:
For checks that support multiple instances (list syntax), tags can be added to each instance:

silver:
  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema
      table: orders
      checks:
        compare_metric:
          - observed:
              metric: count
            expected: 1000
            operator: ">="
            tags: [critical]

          - observed:
              metric: aggregate
              column: amount
              function: sum
            expected: 50000
            operator: ">="
            tags: [daily, finance]

docs.title: Combining with Other Filters
docs.text:
Tags filtering works alongside other filtering options:

# Run critical checks only on silver suite
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    run_suites=["silver"],
    tags=["critical"]
)

# Run daily checks on specific tables
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    selector={"silver": ["orders", "customers"]},
    tags=["daily"]
)

# Exclude expensive tests during smoke runs
results = run_dq(
    "/Workspace/config/",
    tags=["smoke"]  # Checks tagged "expensive" won't run
)

docs.title: Suggested Tag Conventions
docs.text: Tag Description Typical Usage critical Must pass for pipeline to proceed Pre-merge validation smoke Quick sanity checks Fast feedback loops daily Run once per day Scheduled batch jobs hourly Run every hour Near-real-time monitoring expensive Long-running checks Off-peak execution regression Post-deployment validation Release validation finance Financial data checks Audit compliance pii PII-related validations Privacy compliance

docs.title: 1. CI/CD Pipeline Stages
docs.text:
# PR validation - fast checks only
if is_pull_request:
    results = run_dq(config, tags=["smoke", "critical"])

# Post-merge - full validation
else:
    results = run_dq(config)  # All checks

docs.title: 2. Scheduled Jobs
docs.text:
# Hourly job
results = run_dq(config, tags=["hourly"])

# Daily job - includes hourly checks
results = run_dq(config, tags=["daily", "hourly"])

# Weekly full check
results = run_dq(config, tags=["weekly", "expensive"])

docs.title: 3. On-Demand Validation
docs.text:
# Finance team audit
results = run_dq(config, tags=["finance", "critical"])

# Privacy compliance check
results = run_dq(config, tags=["pii"])

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
Tags filtering is optimized for efficiency:

  1. Pre-filtering at orchestrator level: Tables without tagged checks are never loaded
  2. Suite skipping: If no tables remain after filtering, the suite is skipped entirely
  3. Early check filtering: Checks are filtered before execution, not after

This means running tags=["smoke"] on a large configuration will only load and process the relevant subset.

docs.title: Do
docs.text:
• Use consistent tag names across your organization
  • Document your tag conventions in your config repository
  • Combine tags for flexible scheduling (e.g., daily implies critical + daily checks)
  • Use smoke tag for checks that can run in under a minute

docs.title: Don't
docs.text:
• Add tags to every check (defeats the purpose of filtering)
  • Use too many unique tags (becomes hard to manage)
  • Rely solely on tags for critical checks (ensure they run in at least one scheduled job)

docs.title: "No checks match tags filter"
docs.text:
This log message appears when: - No checks in a table have any of the specified tags - The table is skipped to save resources

Solution: Verify that your checks have the expected tags configured.

docs.title: Checks not running
docs.text:
If expected checks aren't running:

  1. Verify the check has tags configured (not just enabled: true)
  2. Remember: checks without tags are skipped when filtering is active
  3. Check for typos in tag names (tags are case-sensitive)

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
Enable verbose logging to see filtering decisions:

results = run_dq(config, tags=["critical"], verbose=True)

Look for log messages like: - Tags filter set: ['critical'] for suite silver - No checks match tags filter for catalog.schema.table, skipping

docs.title: Template System (Planned)
docs.text:
Jinja2-powered configuration templates for generating DQ suite configurations from parameterized patterns.

Planned feature, not yet available

The template system is not implemented and cannot be used today. Everything below (registry, syntax, examples) describes the proposed design, not a shipping feature. Treat the code samples as a spec, not as working config. For multi-environment needs available today, use Profiles, which cover the common parameterization cases.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The template system provides:

  • Jinja2-based YAML generation
  • Tag-based template invocation
  • Loop and conditional logic
  • Centralized template registry

Templates are Jinja2 YAML files that generate complete suite configurations when rendered with context variables.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
config_resolver
  ↓
template_registry.yaml (name → path mapping)
  ↓
*.yaml templates (Jinja2 syntax)
  ↓
rendered config dict
  ↓
orchestrator

Templates are resolved before reaching the orchestrator. Suites receive already-interpreted configuration.

docs.title: Template Registry
docs.text:
The registry maps template tags to file paths.

File: neco_dq/config/template_registry.yaml

silver_standard: config/silver/silver_standard_template.yaml
ge_standard: config/ge/ge_standard_template.yaml

Structure:

  • Keys: template tag (string identifier)
  • Values: relative path from neco_dq package root

Note: Paths in the registry are relative to the neco_dq package directory. For example, config/silver/silver_standard_template.yaml resolves to neco_dq/config/silver/silver_standard_template.yaml in the repository.

New templates must be registered here.

docs.title: Invocation
docs.text:
Templates are invoked by passing the tag to the config resolver.

from neco_dq.config.config_resolver import resolve_config

# Pass template tag as string
config = resolve_config("silver_standard")

# Resolver looks up path in registry and renders template

No separate instance files.

Template tags are passed directly to resolve_config().

docs.title: Template Structure
docs.text: Templates are Jinja2-enhanced YAML files.

docs.title: Minimal Template
docs.text:
silver:
  tables:
{% for t in tables %}
    - catalog: "{{ t.catalog }}"
      schema: "{{ t.schema }}"
      table: "{{ t.table }}"
      checks:
        idempotency:
          key_columns: "{{ t.pk_id }}"
          enabled: true
{% endfor %}

docs.title: Context Variables
docs.text:
Templates receive rendering context from external sources.

Example context:

context = {
    "tables": [
        {"catalog": "main", "schema": "silver", "table": "orders", "pk_id": "order_id"},
        {"catalog": "main", "schema": "silver", "table": "customers", "pk_id": "customer_id"}
    ],
    "data_to_save": [
        {"dq_history_table": "main.dq.history", "dq_alerts_table": "main.dq.alerts"}
    ]
}

Important: Context is provided externally. Templates define structure, not data.

docs.title: Silver Standard Template
docs.text:
File: neco_dq/config/silver/silver_standard_template.yaml

silver:
  tables:
{% for t in tables %}
    - catalog: "{{ t.catalog }}"
      schema: "{{ t.schema }}"
      table: "{{ t.table }}"

      checks:

        idempotency:
          key_column:
          {% if t.pk_id is string %}
            {{ t.pk_id }}
          {% else %}
          {% for c in t.pk_id %}
            - {{ c }}
          {% endfor %}
          {% endif %}
          enabled: true
          blocking: true

{% if t.status_column is defined %}
        status_transition:
          key_columns: "{{ t.pk_id[0] if t.pk_id is not string else t.pk_id }}"
          status_column: "{{ t.status_column }}"
          timestamp_column: "{{ t.timestamp_column }}"
          allowed_flow:
            - CREATED
            - AUTHORIZED
            - CAPTURED
            - FAILED
            - REFUNDED
          enabled: true
          blocking: true
{% endif %}
{% endfor %}

{% for d in data_to_save %}
  data_to_save:
    - table: "{{ d.dq_history_table }}"
      write_mode: append
      alerts: false
      columns_to_save:
        - test_suite
        - catalog
        - schema
        - table
        - run_timestamp
        - passed
{% endfor %}

Key patterns:

  • Loop over tables list
  • Conditional blocks with {% if %}
  • Type checking: is string, is defined
  • Nested attribute access: t.pk_id[0]

docs.title: Great Expectations Standard Template
docs.text:
File: neco_dq/config/ge/ge_standard_template.yaml

great_expectations:
  tables:
{% for t in tables %}
    - catalog: "{{ t.catalog }}"
      schema: "{{ t.schema }}"
      table: "{{ t.table }}"
      checks:
        _dataset:
          min_rows: 1
          severity: error
          blocking: true

{% if t.pk_id is string %}
        {{ t.pk_id }}:
          dtype:
            values: ["str"]
            severity: error
            blocking: true
          nullable:
            enabled: false
          unique:
            enabled: true
            blocking: true
{% else %}
        {{ t.pk_id[0] }}:
          dtype:
            values: ["str"]
            severity: error
            blocking: true
          nullable:
            enabled: false
          unique:
            enabled: true
            blocking: true
            column_list: {{ t.pk_id | tojson }}
{% endif %}
{% endfor %}

{% for d in data_to_save %}
  data_to_save:
    - table: "{{ d.dq_history_table }}"
      write_mode: append
      alerts: false
      merge_schema: true
      columns_to_save:
        - test_suite
        - catalog
        - schema
        - table
        - column
        - run_timestamp
        - passed
        - status
{% endfor %}

Key patterns:

  • Branching on primary key structure (string vs list)
  • Jinja2 filters: | tojson
  • Nested YAML generation
  • Multiple loops for different sections
