docs.title: Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
These patterns are strictly forbidden and will be rejected in code review:

  1. Suite reading YAML - Configuration must be resolved before reaching suites
  2. Suite calling alerts - Alerts are post-execution, orchestrator responsibility
  3. Suite invoking another suite - Suites are independent plugins
  4. Policy logic inside metrics - Metrics compute, policy evaluates
  5. Hardcoded constants replacing config - All behavior via configuration
  6. Special cases in orchestrator - Orchestrator is pure coordinator
  7. Business-specific naming - All checks must be generic and reusable
  8. Cross-layer dependencies - Each layer owns its responsibilities

docs.title: Determinism Requirement
docs.text:
neco_dq guarantees deterministic execution:

Same input + Same config = Same output

This means:

  • No randomness - Results must be reproducible
  • No time-dependent behavior - Unless explicitly configured (e.g., freshness checks)
  • No external dependencies that can change - All inputs must be controlled
  • Reproducible results - For audit, debugging, and regression testing

Any violation of determinism is a bug and must be fixed.

docs.title: Definition of Done
docs.text:
A change is acceptable only if:

  • [ ] Registry works (suites load correctly)
  • [ ] Result contracts unchanged (or explicitly versioned)
  • [ ] Summary can read results
  • [ ] Policies are enforceable
  • [ ] No cross-layer violations
  • [ ] Behavior is reproducible

docs.title: DQ Dashboard (Lakeview)
docs.text: Generate a Databricks AI/BI (Lakeview) dashboard on top of the DQ results history table.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The framework persists every check result to a history table in Unity Catalog. generate_dashboard() builds a ready-to-use Lakeview dashboard on top of that table from a bundled, versioned template: no SQL or widgets are authored by hand; the proven queries are reused verbatim and only the deployment-specific values are filled in.

The dashboard is a single page with 8 datasets feeding widgets for:

Area Widgets Status Pass/Fail pie, tests by layer, tests by table, failed-checks heatmap Coverage Bronze / Silver / Gold coverage pies (expected vs tested) Dimensions DQ Dimension Matrix (completeness, uniqueness, validity, …) Trends Pass-rate, blocking-failures and duration trend lines KPIs Pass rate, blocking failures, tables covered, last run Regression New Failures / Recovered counters + a detail table Filters Layer, Table, Run Date (global)

Top (Status) section: KPIs, filters, pass/fail split and a failed-checks heatmap.

Lower section: coverage per tier, the DQ dimension matrix, regression detail and the trend lines. Both images are illustrative mockups with sample data, not screenshots of a live workspace.

Scope of the whole dashboard = your expected_tables

Every widget is scoped to the exact (schema, table) pairs you declare in expected_tables, not just the coverage pies. A table you do not list is invisible across the entire dashboard. See The expected_tables contract.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A DQ history table already populated by your runs (the target declared in data_to_save).
  • A SQL warehouse id.

This is designed to run inside a Databricks notebook, where nothing extra is needed: databricks-sdk is already installed in the runtime, and WorkspaceClient() (created with no arguments) authenticates automatically from the notebook context, so there are no credentials to set.

Running from outside Databricks

Only if you run this outside a notebook (local machine, CI) do you need to install the SDK and provide credentials via the standard environment variables:

pip install databricks-sdk
export DATABRICKS_HOST=...
export DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID=...
export DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET=...

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
from neco_dq.dashboards import generate_dashboard

result = generate_dashboard(
    history_table="my_catalog.dq.dq_test_history",
    catalog="my_catalog",
    warehouse_id="<warehouse_id>",
    parent_path="/Users/you@org",
    layers={
        "bronze": ["raw"],
        "silver": ["clean"],
        "gold":   ["mart", "marts"],
    },
    expected_tables=[
        ("mart",  "orders"),
        ("mart",  "customers"),
        ("clean", "events"),
    ],
    mode="create",
)

print("dashboard_id:", result["dashboard_id"])

Just run the cell in a Databricks notebook: authentication is automatic. (To run it from outside Databricks instead, see Prerequisites for the credentials setup.)

parent_path with a service principal

If you authenticate as a service principal it may not own a /Users/... folder. Point parent_path at a workspace folder the principal can write to (e.g. a shared folder). Dashboards created via the API are owned by the calling principal; transfer ownership to a human via the UI if needed.

docs.title: generate_dashboard()
docs.text:
Parameter Type Required Default Description history_table str Yes (none) Full 3-part name (catalog.schema.table) used in every dataset's FROM. parent_path str Yes (none) Workspace folder to create the dashboard in (create mode). layers dict[str, list[str] \| dict] Yes (none) Medallion tier → schema(s), optionally per-catalog. See layers. expected_tables list[tuple[str, str] \| tuple[str, str, str]] Yes (none) (schema, table) pairs (catalog resolved from layers) or (catalog, schema, table) triples, scoping the whole dashboard. See contract. catalog str \| None No None Global catalog for list-form layers entries. Required only if at least one tier is a plain schema list. See layers. warehouse_id str \| None No None SQL warehouse for the dashboard + query validation. If omitted, the first RUNNING warehouse is auto-discovered. See note. display_name str No "DQ Dashboard" Dashboard title. dashboard_id str \| None No None Existing dashboard to patch (required for mode="update"). mode str No "create" "create" or "update". See modes. template str No "reference" Which bundled template to hydrate. validate_queries bool No True Run every dataset query on the warehouse before publishing. publish bool No True Publish after create/patch so viewers see the change.

hydrate_template() accepts the same inputs minus the I/O ones (parent_path, dashboard_id, mode, validate_queries, publish) and returns the create/patch payload as a pure function, useful for inspection and testing.

docs.title: layers
docs.text:
Maps each medallion tier to the schema(s) that belong to it. The three tiers bronze / silver / gold are the dashboard's fixed structure (one coverage pie and a layer axis per tier), but which schemas (and which catalog) map to each tier is entirely up to you.

Each tier is given in one of two forms:

layers = {
    # list form: these schemas live in the global `catalog` argument
    "bronze": ["raw"],
    "silver": ["clean"],
    # dict form: this tier lives in its own catalog
    "gold":   {"catalog": "mart_catalog", "schemas": ["mart", "marts"]},
}
  • Same catalog, different schemas per tier: use the list form for every tier and pass a single global catalog. (This is the original behaviour; the catalog argument is unchanged.)
  • Separate catalog per tier: use the dict form for the tiers that live elsewhere. catalog is then needed only if some tier still uses the list form.

Rules:

  • At least one tier must be present; tiers are otherwise optional: a bronze-only dashboard is valid. Absent tiers simply render empty widgets (their coverage pie shows no data) rather than being removed.
  • Each present tier must map to a non-empty schema list.
  • No tier outside bronze / silver / gold is allowed.
  • Catalog and schema names must not contain quotes (rejected as invalid input).
  • A schema name may be declared under two different catalogs (e.g. a raw schema in both bronze_cat and silver_cat). The (catalog, schema) scope keeps them distinct. When this happens, reference those tables in expected_tables with the explicit (catalog, schema, table) triple — a plain (schema, table) pair would be ambiguous and is rejected. See the contract.

layers drives: the (catalog, schema) scope filter, the (catalog, schema)→layer CASE maps (including Great-Expectations rows folded into tiers), and the per-tier coverage pies.

Bronze-only, single catalog

generate_dashboard(
    history_table="my_catalog.dq.dq_test_history",
    catalog="my_catalog",
    parent_path="/Users/you@org",
    layers={"bronze": ["raw"]},
    expected_tables=[("raw", "ingestion")],
)

Each tier in its own catalog

generate_dashboard(
    history_table="meta.dq.dq_test_history",
    parent_path="/Users/you@org",
    layers={
        "bronze": {"catalog": "bronze_cat", "schemas": ["raw"]},
        "silver": {"catalog": "silver_cat", "schemas": ["clean"]},
        "gold":   {"catalog": "gold_cat",   "schemas": ["mart"]},
    },
    expected_tables=[("raw", "ingestion"), ("clean", "events"), ("mart", "orders")],
    # no global `catalog` needed: every tier carries its own
)

docs.title: The expected_tables contract
docs.text:
expected_tables is the single source of truth for the entire dashboard, not just the coverage widget.

expected_tables = [
    ("mart",  "orders"),
    ("mart",  "customers"),
    ("clean", "events"),
]
  • Each entry is either a (schema, table) pair or a (catalog, schema, table) triple (the two forms may be mixed in one list). The list must be non-empty. For a pair, the schema's catalog is resolved automatically from layers, so you don't repeat it. For a triple you give the catalog explicitly.
  • A predicate AND CONCAT(catalog, '.', schema, '.', table) IN (...) is injected into every dataset's base scan, so all widgets (status, KPIs, dimensions, trends, regression, coverage) report on exactly this set, correctly even when the same schema.table name exists in more than one catalog.
  • The coverage pies additionally treat this list as "should exist": a listed table that was never tested shows as not covered.

When to use the triple

Use (schema, table) for the common case — one catalog per schema, resolved from layers. Use (catalog, schema, table) when the same schema name lives in more than one catalog (e.g. a raw schema in both bronze_cat and silver_cat): a bare pair can't tell which one you mean and is rejected as ambiguous, so name the catalog explicitly.

expected_tables = [
    ("mart", "orders"),                 # catalog resolved from layers
    ("bronze_cat", "raw", "ingestion"), # explicit — `raw` exists in 2 catalogs
    ("silver_cat", "raw", "cleaned"),
]

Keep the list curated

A table you omit is completely absent from every widget, not merely excluded from the coverage percentage. Treat expected_tables as your governed catalogue of tables under DQ.

Schema names in expected_tables

Every entry must map to a (catalog, schema) you declared under layers — that's how a table gets a tier for the coverage pies. A pair's schema must be declared in layers; a triple's full (catalog, schema) must be too.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
Mode Behaviour "create" (default) Creates a new dashboard under parent_path. Fails with AlreadyExists if one with the same display_name already exists in that folder. "update" Patches an existing dashboard. Requires dashboard_id.

Re-running against the same dashboard

create is not idempotent: a second create with the same display_name in the same folder fails with AlreadyExists. To update a dashboard you already created, save the dashboard_id from the creation output and call again with mode="update" and that id. There is intentionally no lookup-by-name: the Lakeview list API is eventually consistent (a just-created dashboard may not appear yet), so name-based matching can't be relied on right after a create.

Updating an existing dashboard:

generate_dashboard(
    # ... same coordinates ...
    mode="update",
    dashboard_id="01f...",   # returned at creation time
)

docs.title: Query validation
docs.text:
With validate_queries=True (default) every dataset query is executed on the warehouse before publishing. If any query fails, the call raises RuntimeError and nothing is published.

The sel_date parameter is bound automatically

Seven of the eight datasets reference the :sel_date Run Date parameter. The validator binds sel_date = 'All' (the "unfiltered" sentinel) so a standalone run doesn't fail with UNBOUND_SQL_PARAMETER.

To inspect the generated dashboard without any workspace writes, use the pure function directly:

from neco_dq.dashboards import hydrate_template

payload = hydrate_template(
    history_table="my_catalog.dq.dq_test_history",
    catalog="my_catalog",
    warehouse_id="<warehouse_id>",
    layers={"bronze": ["raw"], "silver": ["clean"], "gold": ["mart"]},
    expected_tables=[("mart", "orders")],
)
print(payload["serialized_dashboard"])   # the fully-hydrated Lakeview JSON

docs.title: Warehouse auto-discovery
docs.text:
warehouse_id is optional. If you omit it, the first RUNNING warehouse in the workspace is used (or the first of any state if none is running):

generate_dashboard(
    history_table="my_catalog.dq.dq_test_history",
    catalog="my_catalog",
    parent_path="/Users/you@org",
    layers={"bronze": ["raw"], "silver": ["clean"], "gold": ["mart"]},
    expected_tables=[("mart", "orders")],
    # warehouse_id omitted → auto-discovered
)

Auto-discovery is not deterministic

It picks whatever RUNNING warehouse comes first. For reproducible runs (CI, jobs), pass warehouse_id explicitly. If the workspace has no warehouse, a RuntimeError is raised.

docs.title: Confirmation output
docs.text:
On success the function prints a terminal confirmation with a direct link to the published dashboard:

   DQ Dashboard generated successfully
   Name:      DQ Dashboard
   ID:        01f2c9...
   Action:    Created + published
   Open:      https://<workspace>.cloud.databricks.com/dashboardsv3/01f2c9.../published

The Action line reflects whether the dashboard was created or updated, and whether it was published (publish=True) or left as a draft.

docs.title: Return value
docs.text:
generate_dashboard() returns a small, curated summary dict, not the raw API response (which embeds the full serialized dashboard JSON, so printing it whole dumps an unreadable wall of text):

Key Example Notes dashboard_id "01f2c9..." The created/updated dashboard id. display_name "DQ Dashboard" Effective title. url https://<workspace>.../dashboardsv3/01f2c9.../published Published link, or None if the host is unknown. action "created" / "updated" Which operation ran. published True / False Whether it was published. 
result = generate_dashboard(...)
print(result["url"])   # clean, one-line link, safe to print whole

docs.title: History table requirements
docs.text:
Every dataset reads from the single history_table. It must expose at least:

Column Type Used for run_timestamp timestamp "latest run per table" (DENSE_RANK), trends, Run Date filter test_suite string bronze / silver / gold / great_expectations catalog, schema, table, column string Entity coordinates + expected_tables matching check_name string Classified into DQ dimensions severity, blocking, passed, status (none) Pass/fail, blocking-failure metrics

Sparse JSON fields

The Execution Duration trend depends on execution:duration_ms, which is sparsely populated; that widget may be mostly empty until the framework consistently emits it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom What's happening / how to fix Empty widgets The table isn't in expected_tables, or its schema isn't mapped in layers. Add it to both. Coverage shows tables as "not covered" Those expected_tables entries have no test results yet, which is normal until they're tested. RuntimeError: dataset query failed [...] A query didn't validate. Double-check history_table, catalog, and that the schemas exist. AlreadyExists: A node with name '...' A dashboard with that display_name is already in parent_path. Re-run with mode="update" + its dashboard_id, or pick a different name (see Modes). Permission error / wrong parent_path Point parent_path at a folder your identity can write to. Entity etag ... does not match (update) Someone changed the dashboard since it was read. Just retry: the call always fetches a fresh version first. ImportError: databricks-sdk Run pip install databricks-sdk.

docs.title: Test Suites Overview
docs.text: Neco DQ groups its checks into suites. Each suite targets a different stage of the medallion architecture and answers a different question about your data. This page helps you pick the right one before diving into its (longer) reference page.

docs.title: Which suite do I need?
docs.text:
Suite Validates Answers the question Typical checks Typical use Bronze Raw data right after ingestion "Did the data arrive, intact and fresh?" record_count, freshness, schema_drift, mandatory_fields, binary payloads Often kept as warnings Silver Cleaned/transformed data "Is the data correct, consistent and referentially sound?" referential_integrity, business_rules, cardinality, compare_metric, cross_table_equality Usually set to block Gold Aggregated business metrics "Do the KPIs reconcile and meet expectations?" reconciliation_expr, compare_metric, coverage, trend, volume Usually set to block Profiling Any table (exploratory) "What does this data look like, and what should I check?" stats + auto-suggested checks Non-blocking by design Great Expectations Column/schema contracts "Does each column honour its declared contract?" not_null, unique, dtype, values_set, date_format Depends on config Custom Anything the built-ins don't "How do I express a rule specific to my domain?" your own Python checks Depends on config

\"Typical use\" is a convention, not a default

Whether a failing check fails the run or only warns is set per check with blocking (default false), governed by the Failure Policy. The column above reflects how teams usually configure each suite, not a built-in behaviour.

docs.title: How to choose
docs.text:
• Following the medallion flow? Use Bronze → Silver → Gold on the matching layers. That's the common path and the three integrate cleanly (Gold checks can reconcile back to Silver).
  • New table, not sure what to check? Start with Profiling in suggest mode: it inspects the data and proposes a starting config you then curate.
  • You think in column contracts (a column must be non-null, an enum, a date in a given format)? Great Expectations is the most natural fit.
  • The rule is domain-specific and no built-in check expresses it? Write a Custom suite.

Suites are independent

You don't have to use all of them. A config can enable just Bronze, or mix Silver + Great Expectations, whatever matches your tables. Every suite writes to the same result contract, one report, and one history table.

docs.title: Shared concepts
docs.text:
These apply across the medallion suites (Bronze/Silver/Gold), so they're documented once:

  • Thresholds: allow a tolerated number or percentage of failing rows before a check fails.
  • Compare Metric: the observed/expected comparison engine used by many Silver and Gold checks.
  • Data Filtering and Tag Filtering: scope which rows and which checks run.
  • Failure Policy: how blocking, severity and the policy engine turn check results into a pass/warn/fail exit code.

docs.title: Next step
docs.text: Pick a suite from the table above, or read Modular Configuration to see how suites, tables and checks fit together in a config tree.

docs.title: Bronze Test Suite
docs.text: The Bronze test suite validates raw data immediately after ingestion from source systems.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
The Bronze suite is:

  • Ingestion-level: Validates data as soon as it lands
  • Technical: No business logic, only technical guarantees
  • Check-centric: Each check produces one result row
  • Cheap and deterministic: Fast, repeatable validations

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Bronze validation ensures:

  • Data arrived from source systems
  • Tables are readable and not empty
  • Data is fresh enough
  • Schema hasn't drifted unexpectedly
  • Mandatory fields are present
  • Binary payloads are valid (if applicable)

Debugging failures

When checks fail, see Debug Experience for understanding failure_stats, investigation_query, and how to investigate.

docs.title: 1. Minimal Example
docs.text:
Use this when you only want to verify that a table exists and is not empty.

bronze:
  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema_bronze
      table: transactions

      checks:
        record_count:
          enabled: true
          severity: warning
          blocking: false

Executed checks: - table_read (implicit, always critical) - record_count

docs.title: 2. Standard Ingestion Checks (Recommended)
docs.text:
Covers the most common ingestion guarantees.

bronze:
  default_checks:
    record_count:
      enabled: true
      severity: warning
      blocking: false

    table_freshness:
      enabled: true
      severity: warning
      blocking: false
      max_staleness_days: 2

  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema_bronze
      table: transactions

Behavior: - default_checks apply to all tables - Each table inherits these checks automatically

docs.title: 3. Table-Level Overrides
docs.text:
Override or extend default checks for a specific table.

bronze:
  default_checks:
    record_count:
      enabled: true
      severity: warning
      blocking: false

  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema_bronze
      table: transactions
      checks:
        freshness:
          enabled: true
          severity: critical
          blocking: true
          timestamp_column: event_timestamp
          max_delay_hours: 6

In this case: - record_count comes from default_checks - freshness is defined only for this specific table

docs.title: Threshold Configuration
docs.text: Row-level checks can tolerate a number or percentage of failing rows via a threshold block. The mechanics (max_failure_percent, max_failure_count, AND logic, suite-level defaults) are the same across suites and documented once in Thresholds. The Bronze-specific part is which checks support it:

docs.title: Supported Bronze Checks
docs.text: Check Supports Threshold mandatory_fields yes json_schema yes (shared check) business_rules yes (shared check) binary_not_null yes binary_non_empty yes binary_size_guard yes binary_decodable yes binary_version_header_check yes binary_schema_fingerprint yes record_count no (binary pass/fail) record_count_anomaly no (uses max_deviation_percent) freshness no (uses max_delay_hours) table_freshness no (uses max_staleness_days) schema_drift no (binary pass/fail) binary_type no (binary pass/fail)

docs.title: Check Reference Table
docs.text:
YAML Check Name Method Invoked Purpose record_count _check_record_count Verify table is not empty record_count_anomaly _check_record_count_anomaly Detect unexpected volume changes freshness _check_freshness Validate data recency (row-level timestamp) table_freshness _check_table_freshness Validate table metadata freshness schema_drift _check_schema_drift Prevent unexpected schema changes mandatory_fields _check_mandatory_fields Ensure required columns exist and are non-null json_schema _check_json_schema Validate JSON column structure (shared check) business_rules _check_business_rules Validate SQL expressions (shared check) binary_not_null _check_binary_not_null Binary column must exist and have no nulls binary_non_empty _check_binary_non_empty Binary payloads must not be empty binary_size_guard _check_binary_size_guard Validate binary payload size bounds binary_type _check_binary_type Ensure column has binary data type binary_decodable _check_binary_decodable Verify binary payload can be decoded binary_version_header_check _check_binary_version_header_check Validate binary header structure binary_schema_fingerprint _check_binary_schema_fingerprint Ensure binary schema conformity partition_exists _check_partition_exists Verify expected partitions exist

Each enabled check: - Produces one output row - Has its own severity and blocking behavior

docs.title: record_count
docs.text:
Purpose: Verifies that the table contains at least one record.

What it does: - Executes a count() on the DataFrame - Fails if the table is empty

Typical use: - Detect missing or failed ingestions - Ensure upstream pipelines actually produced data

Notes: - Very lightweight check - Often enabled by default in Bronze - Can be blocking in critical ingestion paths

Example:

record_count:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Record count OK: 15000 rows FAIL Table empty: 0 rows

docs.title: record_count_anomaly
docs.text:
Purpose: Detects unexpected changes in record volume compared to previous runs.

What it does: - Reads the last recorded record_count from the configured history table - Compares current row count with the previous value - Fails if the deviation exceeds a configurable percentage

Key configuration: - history_table: table used to retrieve historical values - max_deviation_percent (default: 40%)

Typical use: - Catch partial loads or duplicates - Early anomaly detection in ingestion pipelines

Notes: - Automatically passes if no history is available

Example:

record_count_anomaly:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  history_table: my_dq_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history
  max_deviation_percent: 40

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Record count OK: 15000 (deviation 12.5% within 40% limit) PASS No history configured PASS No previous value in history FAIL Count deviation 65.3% exceeds 40% limit

docs.title: freshness
docs.text:
Purpose: Ensures data is recent based on a timestamp column inside the table.

What it does: - Computes the maximum value of a configured timestamp column - Compares it to the current time (UTC) - Fails if the delay exceeds the allowed threshold

Key configuration: - timestamp_column: column containing timestamps (TIMESTAMP or DATE; a date is read as midnight UTC of that day) - max_delay_hours (default: 24)

Typical use: - Validate that upstream systems are still publishing data - Enforce SLAs on event-time freshness

Example:

freshness:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  timestamp_column: updated_at
  max_delay_hours: 24

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Data fresh: 2.3h old (within 24h limit) FAIL Data age 48.5h exceeds 24h limit FAIL No data found in column 'updated_at'

docs.title: table_freshness
docs.text:
Purpose: Checks freshness based on table metadata rather than row-level timestamps.

What it does: - Reads lastModified from DESCRIBE DETAIL - Computes how many days the table has been stale - Fails if it exceeds the configured threshold

Key configuration: - max_staleness_days (default: 2)

Typical use: - Validate batch pipelines - Useful when tables do not contain reliable timestamp columns

Example:

table_freshness:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  max_staleness_days: 2

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Table fresh: updated 8.5h ago (within 2d limit) FAIL Table stale: 72.3h since update exceeds 2d limit

docs.title: schema_drift
docs.text:
Purpose: Prevents unexpected schema changes from propagating downstream.

What it does: - Compares the actual table schema with an expected schema definition - Detects: - Missing columns - Type mismatches

Key configuration: - expected_columns: dictionary mapping column names to expected types

Typical use: - Protect Silver and Gold layers - Enforce schema contracts across teams

Notes: - Frequently configured as blocking in Silver/Gold

Example:

schema_drift:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  expected_columns:
    id: string
    created_at: timestamp
    amount: double

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Schema OK: 5 columns verified FAIL Schema issues: 2 missing, 1 type mismatch

docs.title: mandatory_fields
docs.text:
Purpose: Ensures that required columns are present and non-null.

What it does: - Verifies column existence - Checks for null values in mandatory columns

Key configuration: - columns: list of mandatory column names - threshold (optional): failure tolerance - max_failure_percent: maximum allowed percentage of null rows (0-100) - max_failure_count: maximum allowed number of null rows

Result details: violated_columns=[...]

Typical use: - Enforce minimum data completeness - Validate business-critical attributes

Example:

mandatory_fields:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  columns:
    - id
    - created_at
    - amount

Example with threshold:

mandatory_fields:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  columns:
    - id
    - created_at
  threshold:
    max_failure_percent: 1.0  # Allow up to 1% null rows

Example Output:

Status Details PASS All 3 mandatory columns present and non-null FAIL Found 150 null values (1.5% of 10000) FAIL Missing 2 required columns

docs.title: Binary Payload Checks
docs.text: These checks are specialized for validating binary columns (e.g., serialized Avro, Protobuf, encoded JSON).

docs.title: binary_not_null
docs.text:
Purpose: Ensures that the specified binary column exists and contains no nulls.

What it does: - Verifies that the column exists - Counts null values - Returns pass/fail depending on whether any nulls are present

Key configuration: - column: binary column to check - threshold (optional): failure tolerance - max_failure_percent: maximum allowed percentage of null rows (0-100) - max_failure_count: maximum allowed number of null rows

Result details: null_count: <number_of_null_values>

Typical use: - Enforce minimum data completeness in binary columns - Ensure critical binary payloads are not missing

Example:

binary_not_null:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  column: payload_bin

Example with threshold:

binary_not_null:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  column: payload_bin
  threshold:
    max_failure_count: 10  # Allow up to 10 null payloads

Example Output:

Status Details PASS All values non-null in 'payload_bin' FAIL Found 25 null values (0.5% of 5000) FAIL Column not found: 'payload_bin'

docs.title: binary_non_empty
docs.text:
Purpose: Ensures that binary column contains non-empty payloads.

What it does: - Verifies column existence - Counts rows with zero-length binary values - Returns pass/fail depending on whether any empty values exist

Key configuration: - column: binary column to check - threshold (optional): failure tolerance - max_failure_percent: maximum allowed percentage of empty rows (0-100) - max_failure_count: maximum allowed number of empty rows

Result details: empty_binary_count: <number_of_empty_values>

Typical use: - Validate payload presence - Detect incomplete or placeholder binary data

Example:

binary_non_empty:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  column: payload_bin

Example with threshold:

binary_non_empty:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  column: payload_bin
  threshold:
    max_failure_percent: 0.5  # Allow up to 0.5% empty payloads

Example Output:

Status Details PASS All values non-empty in 'payload_bin' FAIL Found 12 empty values (0.24% of 5000)

docs.title: binary_size_guard
docs.text:
Purpose: Ensures binary payloads fall within expected size limits.

What it does: - Verifies column existence - Checks that each payload length is between min_bytes and max_bytes

Key configuration: - column: binary column to check - min_bytes (optional): minimum allowed length - max_bytes (optional): maximum allowed length - threshold (optional): failure tolerance - max_failure_percent: maximum allowed percentage of invalid rows (0-100) - max_failure_count: maximum allowed number of invalid rows

Result details: invalid_size_count: <number_of_invalid_payloads>

Typical use: - Protect downstream consumers from undersized or oversized payloads - Enforce schema consistency

Example:

binary_size_guard:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  column: payload_bin
  min_bytes: 5
  max_bytes: 1024

Example with threshold:

binary_size_guard:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  column: payload_bin
  min_bytes: 5
  max_bytes: 1024
  threshold:
    max_failure_percent: 2.0  # Allow up to 2% out-of-bounds payloads

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Binary size OK in 'payload_bin' (min=5B, max=1024B) FAIL Found 45 size violations (0.9% of 5000)

docs.title: binary_type
docs.text:
Purpose: Ensures the column has binary data type.

What it does: - Checks if column exists - Verifies Spark type is BinaryType

Key configuration: - column: binary column to check

Result details: type: <actual_spark_data_type>

Typical use: - Validate column type against expected schema - Prevent accidental type mismatches (string, integer, etc.)

Example:

binary_type:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  column: payload_bin

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Type OK: 'payload_bin' is binary FAIL Type mismatch: expected binary, got string FAIL Column not found: 'payload_bin'

docs.title: binary_decodable
docs.text:
Purpose: Ensures binary payload can be decoded according to a specified format.

What it does: - Verifies column existence - Supports decoding formats: json, base64_json, avro, protobuf - Counts invalid payloads (undecodable or malformed)

Key configuration: - column: binary column to check - format: decoding format (json, base64_json, avro, protobuf) - threshold (optional): failure tolerance - max_failure_percent: maximum allowed percentage of invalid rows (0-100) - max_failure_count: maximum allowed number of invalid rows

Result details: invalid_payloads: <number_of_invalid_rows>

Typical use: - Validate payload integrity before parsing downstream - Detect corrupt, truncated, or improperly encoded data

Example:

binary_decodable:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  column: payload_bin
  format: base64_json

Example with threshold:

binary_decodable:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  column: payload_bin
  format: base64_json
  threshold:
    max_failure_count: 100  # Allow up to 100 invalid payloads

Example Output:

Status Details PASS All rows decodable as base64_json FAIL Found 78 decode failures (base64_json) (1.6% of 5000) FAIL Invalid format: 'xml' not supported

docs.title: binary_version_header_check
docs.text:
Purpose: Validates binary payload header, checking magic byte and minimum size.

What it does: - Verifies column existence - Ensures payload is at least header_size_bytes long - Compares first byte against magic_byte

Key configuration: - column: binary column to check - magic_byte: expected first byte (integer) - header_size_bytes: minimum header length - threshold (optional): failure tolerance - max_failure_percent: maximum allowed percentage of invalid rows (0-100) - max_failure_count: maximum allowed number of invalid rows

Result details: - too_short: <number_of_short_payloads> - invalid_magic: <number_of_invalid_headers>

Typical use: - Enforce versioning or signature validation in binary payloads - Detect malformed headers or incompatible versions

Example:

binary_version_header_check:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  column: payload_bin
  magic_byte: 0
  header_size_bytes: 5

Example with threshold:

binary_version_header_check:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  column: payload_bin
  magic_byte: 0
  header_size_bytes: 5
  threshold:
    max_failure_percent: 1.0  # Allow up to 1% header violations

Example Output:

Status Details PASS All headers valid (magic=0, size>=5B) FAIL Found 34 invalid headers (0.7% of 5000)

docs.title: binary_schema_fingerprint
docs.text:
Purpose: Ensures that binary payloads conform to an expected schema fingerprint.

What it does: - Computes a fingerprint from a slice of the binary column (offset + length) - Converts the extracted bytes to hexadecimal - Compares each fingerprint against a list of allowed fingerprints - Collects invalid fingerprints for reporting

Key configuration: - column: the binary column to inspect - allowed_fingerprints: list of valid fingerprints (hex, case-insensitive) - offset (optional, default=2): start byte (1-based) for fingerprint extraction - length_bytes (optional, default=4): number of bytes to extract - threshold (optional): failure tolerance - max_failure_percent: maximum allowed percentage of invalid rows (0-100) - max_failure_count: maximum allowed number of invalid rows

Result details: invalid_values: <list_of_invalid_fingerprints>

Typical use: - Validate binary payloads for schema conformity - Enforce standardization on payload structures

Example:

binary_schema_fingerprint:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  column: payload_bin
  allowed_fingerprints:
    - "0013010D"
    - "12D685AA"
    - "12D685BB"
    - "12D685CC"
    - "FFFFFFFF"
  offset: 2
  length_bytes: 4

Example with threshold:

binary_schema_fingerprint:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  column: payload_bin
  allowed_fingerprints:
    - "0013010D"
    - "12D685AA"
  offset: 2
  length_bytes: 4
  threshold:
    max_failure_percent: 0.1  # Allow up to 0.1% unknown fingerprints

Example Output:

Status Details PASS All fingerprints valid (5 allowed) FAIL Found 23 invalid fingerprints (0.5% of 5000)

docs.title: partition_exists
docs.text:
Purpose: Verifies that expected partitions exist in a Delta table.

What it does: - Queries Delta table metadata for existing partitions - Compares against expected partition specifications - Supports both multi-column partitions and single-column checks

Key configuration (Option 1 - Multiple partitions): - partitions: List of partition specifications (e.g., [{year: 2024, month: 1}, {year: 2024, month: 2}])

Key configuration (Option 2 - Single column): - partition_column: Single partition column name - expected_values: List of expected values for that column

Result details: expected=<count>; missing=<count>; missing_partitions=[...]

Typical use: - Validate that expected data partitions have been loaded - Verify daily/monthly partition availability - Detect missing or incomplete data loads

Example 1: Multi-column partitions

partition_exists:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  partitions:
    - year: 2024
      month: 1
    - year: 2024
      month: 2

Example 2: Single column with expected values

partition_exists:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  partition_column: date
  expected_values:
    - "2024-01-01"
    - "2024-01-02"
    - "2024-01-03"

Example Output:

Status Details PASS All 3 expected partitions exist PASS All 5 expected date values exist FAIL Missing 2 expected partitions FAIL Missing 1 date partitions FAIL Table is not partitioned

docs.title: Shared Checks
docs.text: json_schema and business_rules are shared checks (from SharedChecksMixin, composed into every suite) also available at the Bronze layer. At Bronze they are intended for structural / technical validation of raw payloads, not domain logic, which belongs in Silver/Gold (see Design Guidelines). The configuration is identical across suites; the full reference lives in Silver › json_schema and Silver › business_rules.

docs.title: json_schema
docs.text:
Purpose: Validates JSON column structure, required fields, field types, and allowed values, useful for raw API/event payloads landed in Bronze.

Key configuration: - column: JSON column name (required) - required_fields: List of fields that must exist (optional, supports dot-notation) - field_types: Dict of field -> expected type (optional) - allowed_values: Dict of field -> allowed value list (optional) - array_element: If true, validates array elements (default: true) - sample_size: Rows to sample for validation (default: 1000, 0 = all) - max_parse_failure_percent: Max percentage of rows that may fail JSON parsing before the check hard-fails (default: 0) - threshold: Optional threshold configuration (max_failure_percent, max_failure_count)

Example:

json_schema:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  column: raw_payload
  required_fields:
    - event_id
    - event_type
    - payload.source    # Nested field validation
  field_types:
    event_id: string
    retry_count: int
  threshold:
    max_failure_percent: 5.0  # Tolerate up to 5% malformed payloads at ingestion

Example Output:

Status Details PASS JSON schema OK: 5000 elements validated FAIL JSON validation failed: 2 missing fields, 1 type mismatches in 'raw_payload' FAIL JSON parse failed: 50 rows (1.0%) exceed 0% limit

docs.title: business_rules
docs.text:
Purpose: Validates that rows satisfy a SQL boolean expression. At Bronze keep predicates technical (payload sanity, format bounds, non-null invariants) rather than business logic.

Key configuration: - predicate: SQL boolean expression that must be true for every row (required) - name: Human-readable name for the rule (default: "business_rule") - threshold: Optional threshold configuration (max_failure_percent, max_failure_count)

Example:

business_rules:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  name: ingested_at_present
  predicate: "ingested_at IS NOT NULL AND length(raw_payload) > 0"
  threshold:
    max_failure_percent: 1.0  # Tolerate up to 1% malformed records

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Rule 'ingested_at_present' passed (10000 rows) FAIL Found 150 rows violating rule 'ingested_at_present' (1.5% of 10000)

docs.title: Do
docs.text:
• Keep checks cheap and deterministic: Bronze checks should execute quickly and produce consistent results
  • Prefer warning over critical: Unless ingestion must stop, use warning severity
  • Use default_checks: Define common checks once and apply to all tables
  • Focus on technical validation: Schema, volume, freshness, data types

docs.title: Avoid
docs.text:
• Encode business logic in Bronze: Business rules belong in Silver/Gold
  • Create cross-table dependencies: Each table should validate independently
  • Over-configure blocking checks: Too many blocking checks can halt pipelines unnecessarily

docs.title: Typical Evolution Pattern
docs.text:
Bronze → Silver → Gold

Bronze: Data landed correctly (technical) Silver: Data is correct (quality) Gold: Data makes sense (business)

This separation is intentional and enforced by the framework design.

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
Full Bronze configuration for a sales ingestion pipeline:

bronze:
  # Default checks applied to all tables
  default_checks:
    record_count:
      enabled: true
      severity: warning
      blocking: false

    table_freshness:
      enabled: true
      severity: warning
      blocking: false
      max_staleness_days: 2

    record_count_anomaly:
      enabled: true
      severity: warning
      blocking: false
      history_table: my_dq_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history
      max_deviation_percent: 40

  # Tables with specific overrides
  tables:
    # Standard table
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema_bronze
      table: transactions

    # Table with custom freshness check
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema_bronze
      table: events
      checks:
        freshness:
          enabled: true
          severity: critical
          blocking: true
          timestamp_column: event_timestamp
          max_delay_hours: 6

    # Table with binary payload validation
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema_bronze
      table: raw_payloads
      checks:
        binary_not_null:
          enabled: true
          severity: critical
          blocking: true
          column: payload_bin

        binary_decodable:
          enabled: true
          severity: critical
          blocking: true
          column: payload_bin
          format: base64_json

        binary_schema_fingerprint:
          enabled: true
          severity: critical
          blocking: true
          column: payload_bin
          allowed_fingerprints:
            - "0013010D"
            - "12D685AA"
          offset: 2
          length_bytes: 4

docs.title: See Also
docs.text:
• Silver Suite - Next validation layer
  • Configuration Guide - How to structure configs
  • Architecture Overview - Framework design

docs.title: Custom Test Suites
docs.text: Create your own test suites with custom checks tailored to your specific data quality requirements.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The custom_suite_files parameter in run_dq() allows you to load custom test suites from Python files. This enables:

  • Custom validation logic specific to your domain
  • Reusable checks across multiple tables
  • Extension of the built-in suite functionality

Debugging failures

When checks fail, see Debug Experience for understanding failure_stats, investigation_query, and how to investigate.

docs.title: 1. Create the Custom Suite File
docs.text:
# /Workspace/Users/your_user/my_custom_suite.py

from neco_dq.test_suites.base_test_suite import DQTestSuite
from neco_dq.core.io.result_writer import DQResultWriter


class MyCustomSuite(DQTestSuite):
    """Custom test suite for domain-specific validations."""

    def __init__(self, spark, cfg: dict):
        self.spark = spark
        self.cfg = cfg
        self.writer = DQResultWriter(spark)

    @property
    def _suite_name(self) -> str:
        return "my_custom"

    @property
    def _suite_config_key(self) -> str:
        return "my_custom"

    # Define your custom checks as _check_<name> methods
    def _check_custom_validation(self, df, cfg):
        """
        Custom check example.

        Args:
            df: Spark DataFrame
            cfg: Check configuration from YAML

        Returns:
            tuple of (passed: bool, details: str, column: str | None)
        """
        column = cfg.get("column")
        threshold = cfg.get("threshold", 0)

        # Your validation logic here
        null_count = df.filter(df[column].isNull()).count()
        total_count = df.count()

        passed = null_count <= threshold

        # Narrative details format (v1.1.0+)
        if passed:
            details = f"All {total_count} values valid in {column}"
        else:
            pct = null_count / total_count * 100 if total_count > 0 else 0
            details = f"Found {null_count} null values ({pct:.1f}% of {total_count})"

        return passed, details, column

Example Output:

Status Details PASS All 5000 values valid in important_column FAIL Found 25 null values (0.5% of 5000)

docs.title: 2. Create the YAML Configuration
docs.text:
# dq-config/my_custom.yaml

my_custom:
  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema
      table: my_table
      checks:
        custom_validation:
          enabled: true
          column: important_column
          threshold: 10
          severity: error
          blocking: true

docs.title: 3. Run with Custom Suite
docs.text:
from neco_dq.runner import run_dq

# Single custom suite
results = run_dq(
    config_ref="/Workspace/Users/your_user/dq-config/",
    custom_suite_files="/Workspace/Users/your_user/my_custom_suite.py"
)

# Multiple custom suites
results = run_dq(
    config_ref="/Workspace/Users/your_user/dq-config/",
    custom_suite_files=[
        "/Workspace/Users/your_user/order_checks.py",
        "/Workspace/Users/your_user/customer_checks.py",
    ]
)

docs.title: Suite Naming Convention
docs.text:
The suite name is automatically derived from your class name:

Class Name Suite Config Key MyCustomSuite my_custom DataQualityChecksSuite data_quality_checks OrderValidationDQTestSuite order_validation

The following suffixes are removed: DQTestSuite, TestSuite, Suite

docs.title: Check Method Signature
docs.text:
All check methods must follow this pattern:

def _check_<name>(self, df, cfg) -> tuple[bool, str, str | None]:
    """
    Args:
        df: Spark DataFrame (filtered if filters configured)
        cfg: Dict with check configuration from YAML

    Returns:
        - passed: True if check passes
        - details: String with check details for reporting
        - column: Column name (optional, for column-specific checks)
    """
    pass

docs.title: Using Base Suite Features
docs.text: Your custom suite inherits all features from DQTestSuite:

docs.title: Threshold Evaluation
docs.text:
def _check_with_threshold(self, df, cfg):
    failed_count = df.filter("condition").count()
    total_count = df.count()

    # Uses threshold from config or suite defaults
    passed, metadata = self._evaluate_threshold(failed_count, total_count, cfg)
    details = self._build_threshold_details(f"failed={failed_count}", metadata)

    return passed, details, None

docs.title: Data Filtering
docs.text:
Filters are automatically applied before your check runs:

my_custom:
  defaults:
    partition_filter:
      date: "2024-01-15"
    row_filter: "status = 'active'"
  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema
      table: my_table
      # Table-level filters override defaults
      partition_filter:
        date: ["2024-01-14", "2024-01-15"]

docs.title: Helper Methods
docs.text:
# Validate required config keys
valid, error = self._require_cfg(cfg, "column", "threshold")
if not valid:
    return False, error, None

# Get severity and blocking from config
severity = self._severity(cfg)  # default: "warning"
blocking = self._blocking(cfg)  # default: False

# Build narrative details (v1.1.0+)
# PASS: "All 5000 keys unique"
# FAIL: "Found 50 duplicate keys (5.0% of 1000)"
pct = failed_count / total_count * 100 if total_count > 0 else 0
details = f"Found {failed_count} invalid rows ({pct:.1f}% of {total_count})"

# Build debug fields for failures (v1.1.0+)
failure_stats = self._build_failure_stats(
    failure_type="validation_error",
    affected_columns=[column],
    failure_count=failed_count,
    total_checked=total_count,
    diagnostic={"threshold": threshold}
)

investigation_query = self._build_investigation_query(
    check_type="generic",
    table_fq=f"{cfg['catalog']}.{cfg['schema']}.{cfg['table']}",
    affected_columns=[column],
    cfg=cfg
)

execution = self._build_execution_trace(
    start_time=start_time,
    rows_scanned=total_count
)

docs.title: Custom Suite with Multiple Checks
docs.text:
# my_domain_suite.py

from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from neco_dq.test_suites.base_test_suite import DQTestSuite
from neco_dq.core.io.result_writer import DQResultWriter


class MyDomainSuite(DQTestSuite):
    """Domain-specific data quality checks."""

    def __init__(self, spark, cfg: dict):
        self.spark = spark
        self.cfg = cfg
        self.writer = DQResultWriter(spark)

    @property
    def _suite_name(self) -> str:
        return "my_domain"

    @property
    def _suite_config_key(self) -> str:
        return "my_domain"

    def _check_positive_amounts(self, df, cfg):
        """Verify all amounts are positive."""
        column = cfg.get("column", "amount")

        negative_count = df.filter(F.col(column) < 0).count()
        total = df.count()

        passed, meta = self._evaluate_threshold(negative_count, total, cfg)

        # Narrative details format (v1.1.0+)
        if passed:
            details = f"All {total} amounts positive"
        else:
            pct = negative_count / total * 100 if total > 0 else 0
            details = f"Found {negative_count} negative amounts ({pct:.1f}% of {total})"

        return passed, details, column

    def _check_valid_status(self, df, cfg):
        """Verify status values are in allowed list."""
        column = cfg.get("column", "status")
        allowed = cfg.get("allowed_values", [])

        invalid = df.filter(~F.col(column).isin(allowed))
        invalid_count = invalid.count()
        total = df.count()

        passed = invalid_count == 0

        # Narrative details format (v1.1.0+)
        if passed:
            details = f"All {total} status values valid"
        else:
            details = f"Found {invalid_count} invalid status values"

        return passed, details, column

    def _check_date_sequence(self, df, cfg):
        """Verify date columns are in correct sequence."""
        start_col = cfg.get("start_column")
        end_col = cfg.get("end_column")

        valid, error = self._require_cfg(cfg, "start_column", "end_column")
        if not valid:
            return False, error, None

        invalid = df.filter(F.col(start_col) > F.col(end_col))
        invalid_count = invalid.count()
        total = df.count()

        passed = invalid_count == 0

        # Narrative details format (v1.1.0+)
        if passed:
            details = f"All {total} date sequences valid"
        else:
            details = f"Found {invalid_count} invalid date sequences ({start_col} > {end_col})"

        return passed, details, f"{start_col},{end_col}"

Example Output for custom checks:

Check Status Details positive_amounts PASS All 10000 amounts positive positive_amounts FAIL Found 15 negative amounts (0.15% of 10000) valid_status PASS All 10000 status values valid valid_status FAIL Found 8 invalid status values date_sequence PASS All 10000 date sequences valid date_sequence FAIL Found 3 invalid date sequences (created_at > updated_at)

# Run all suites (including custom)
results = run_dq(

docs.title: Name Mapping
docs.text:
The suite directory name must match the _suite_config_key from your Python class:

Python Class _suite_config_key Directory Name OrderChecksSuite order_checks suites/order_checks/ CustomerChecksSuite customer_checks suites/customer_checks/

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Single Responsibility: Each check should validate one specific aspect
  2. Clear Details: Include all relevant counts and thresholds in details
  3. Use Thresholds: Use _evaluate_threshold() for flexible pass/fail criteria
  4. Validate Config: Use _require_cfg() to fail gracefully on missing config
  5. Column Attribution: Return the column name for column-specific checks
  6. Reuse Helpers: Use base class methods for consistent behavior

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Each file must contain exactly one DQTestSuite subclass
  • Each suite must implement _suite_name and _suite_config_key properties
  • Suite names must be unique across all loaded files

docs.title: Gold Test Suite
docs.text: The Gold test suite validates aggregated business metrics and final outputs ready for consumption by analytics, reporting, and ML systems.

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text:
The Gold suite is:

  • Business-metric focused: Validates KPIs and business metrics
  • Reconciliation-oriented: Ensures consistency with Silver layer
  • Aggregation-aware: Validates computed aggregations and rollups
  • KPI- and reporting-ready: Ensures data meets business requirements
  • Check-centric: Each check produces one result row

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Gold validation ensures:

  • Business metrics are numerically correct
  • Aggregations reconcile with Silver source data
  • KPIs meet business expectations and targets
  • Metrics are internally consistent
  • Data is fresh and ready for consumption

Debugging failures

When checks fail, see Debug Experience for understanding failure_stats, investigation_query, and how to investigate.

docs.title: 1. Minimal Example
docs.text:
Use this when you want to enforce a single business guarantee, such as freshness or a basic metric comparison.

gold:
  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema_gold
      table: payments
      checks:
        freshness:
          enabled: true
          severity: critical
          blocking: true
          timestamp_column: paid_at
          max_delay_hours: 24

Executed checks: - table_read (implicit, always critical) - freshness

docs.title: 2. Standard Gold Checks (Recommended)
docs.text:
Covers the most common Gold-layer guarantees: metric validation and reconciliation with Silver.

gold:
  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema_gold
      table: payments
      checks:
        compare_metric:
          enabled: true
          severity: critical
          blocking: true
          metric:
            type: sum
            column: amount
          value: 100000
          operator: ">="

        reconciliation_expr:
          enabled: true
          severity: critical
          blocking: true
          silver:
            catalog: my_catalog
            schema: my_schema_silver
            table: payments
          gold_expr: amount
          silver_expr: amount
          tolerance_percent: 0.01

Behavior: - Validates business metrics meet thresholds - Reconciles aggregated Gold values against Silver source - Typically blocking: true and severity: critical for financial metrics

docs.title: 3. Multiple Check Instances (Advanced)
docs.text:
Gold checks support multiple instances of the same check, for example validating metrics at different aggregation levels.

gold:
  tables:
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema_gold
      table: payments
      checks:
        compare_metric:
          - enabled: true
            severity: critical
            blocking: true
            metric:
              type: sum
              column: amount
            value: 100000
            operator: ">="

          - enabled: true
            severity: warning
            blocking: false
            metric:
              type: count
            value: 1000
            operator: ">="

Each instance produces one independent result row.

docs.title: Threshold Configuration
docs.text: Row-level checks can tolerate a number or percentage of failing rows via a threshold block. The mechanics (max_failure_percent, max_failure_count, AND logic, suite-level defaults) are the same across suites and documented once in Thresholds. The Gold-specific part is which checks support it:

docs.title: Supported Gold Checks
docs.text: Check Supports Threshold uniqueness yes business_rules yes (shared check) json_schema yes (shared check) compare_metric no (uses operators and value tolerance) reconciliation_expr no (uses tolerance_percent) referential_integrity no (strict: fails if any FK is missing) coverage no (uses tolerance_percent) volume no (uses min_value/max_value bounds or history tolerance_percent) freshness no (uses max_delay_hours) cross_gold no (uses tolerance_abs) completeness no (binary pass/fail) trend no (uses history deviation) distinct_count no (binary pass/fail)

docs.title: How YAML Maps to Code
docs.text:
YAML Check Name Method Invoked Purpose business_rules _check_business_rules Validates custom business expressions at row level compare_metric _check_compare_metric Compares observed metrics with expected values reconciliation_expr _check_reconciliation_expr Reconciles aggregated Gold values against Silver referential_integrity _check_referential_integrity Ensures Gold foreign keys exist in Silver uniqueness _check_uniqueness Ensures uniqueness of Gold-level keys coverage _check_coverage Validates Gold metrics sufficiently cover Silver metrics volume _check_volume Detects anomalous variations of volume metrics freshness _check_freshness Ensures Gold data is up to date cross_gold _check_cross_gold Compares metrics across two Gold tables completeness _check_completeness Verify expected dimension values are present trend _check_trend Verify metric trend against history distinct_count _check_distinct_count Validate distinct value count json_schema _check_json_schema Validate JSON column structure

Each enabled check: - Produces one output row per instance - Has its own severity and blocking behavior - May reference Silver or other Gold tables

docs.title: business_rules
docs.text:
Purpose: Validates custom business expressions at row level.

What it does: - Applies SQL expressions to each row - Validates business logic and constraints - Fails if any row violates the rule

Key configuration: - name: descriptive name for the rule - predicate: SQL expression that must evaluate to true - threshold (optional): failure tolerance - max_failure_percent: maximum allowed percentage of failed rows (0-100) - max_failure_count: maximum allowed number of failed rows

Result details: failed_rows=<count>; expression=<check>

Typical use: - Enforce business constraints - Validate calculated fields - Check derived metrics

Example:

business_rules:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  name: amount_and_currency_valid
  predicate: "amount >= 0 AND currency IS NOT NULL"

Example with threshold:

business_rules:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  name: amount_positive
  predicate: "amount >= 0"
  threshold:
    max_failure_percent: 1.0  # Allow up to 1% rule violations

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Rule 'amount_and_currency_valid' passed (5000 rows) FAIL Found 45 rows violating rule 'amount_positive' (0.9% of 5000)

docs.title: compare_metric
docs.text:
Purpose: Compares observed metrics with expected values.

Full Reference

For complete documentation including array statistics, Kendall's W, Borda Count, and advanced examples, see Compare Metric Reference.

What it does: - Computes an observed metric (count, sum, avg, countDistinct, etc.) - Compares against expected value or metric - Supports operators: ==, >=, <=, !=, <, > - Optional group_by for grouped comparisons

Key configuration: - metric: observed metric definition (type, column, optional function) - value: expected static value (if comparing to constant) - expected_from: expected metric definition (if comparing to another metric) - operator: comparison operator - group_by (optional): columns to group by - name (optional): descriptive name

Result details: observed=<value>; expected=<value>; operator=<op>

Typical use: - Validate business thresholds - Compare metrics across tables - Validate KPIs

Example 1: Compare to constant

compare_metric:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  metric:
    type: sum
    column: amount
  value: 100000
  operator: ">="

Example 2: Compare to another metric

compare_metric:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  metric:
    type: aggregate
    function: countDistinct
    column: answer_id
  operator: ">="
  expected_from:
    type: aggregate
    function: countDistinct
    column: product_id
    table: questions
    schema: my_schema_silver

Example 3: Compare array size to table count

compare_metric:
  enabled: true
  severity: error
  blocking: true
  name: products_vs_orders_per_region

  # Observed: number of questions per order_id from JSON array
  metric:
    type: size_array
    column: metadata
    group_by:
      - order_id

  # Expected: number of orders per order_id from orders table
  expected_from:
    type: aggregate
    catalog: my_catalog
    schema: my_schema_silver
    table: orders
    column: product_id
    function: countDistinct
    group_by:
      - order_id

  operator: "=="

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Metric 'total_amount_threshold' OK: 150000 >= 100000 PASS Metric 'products_vs_orders_per_region' OK: 50/50 groups satisfy == FAIL Metric 'payment_count_threshold' expected 1000, got 850 FAIL Found 5 groups failing metric 'products_vs_orders_per_region' (10% of 50)

docs.title: reconciliation_expr
docs.text:
Purpose: Reconciles aggregated Gold values against Silver values.

What it does: - Aggregates Gold data using provided expression - Aggregates Silver source data using provided expression - Compares aggregated values - Allows configurable tolerance for floating-point differences

Key configuration: - silver: Silver table location, as a nested block with catalog, schema, table - gold_expr: SQL expression to aggregate Gold data - silver_expr: SQL expression to aggregate Silver data - group_by (optional): columns to group by for reconciliation - gold_join_columns / silver_join_columns (optional): restrict Silver to the keys present in Gold; one column or a list, paired by position (same length) - tolerance_percent: acceptable percentage difference (default: 1.0) - name (optional): descriptive name

Result details: mismatched_groups=<count>; max_diff=<amount>

Typical use: - Validate Gold aggregations match Silver source - Ensure no data loss in aggregation - Detect calculation errors

Example:

reconciliation_expr:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  name: customers_reconciliation

  silver:

    catalog: my_catalog

    schema: my_schema_silver

    table: orders

  gold_expr: "SUM(unique_customers)"
  silver_expr: "COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)"

  group_by:
    - order_id

  tolerance_percent: 5.0

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Reconciliation OK: gold=15000, silver=15000 (diff 0.0%) PASS All 100 groups reconcile (within 5%) FAIL Reconciliation deviation 12.5% exceeds 5% limit FAIL Found 8 groups exceeding 5% deviation (8% of 100)

docs.title: referential_integrity
docs.text:
Purpose: Ensures Gold foreign keys exist in Silver.

What it does: - Joins Gold and Silver tables - Identifies orphaned Gold records - Fails if any Gold foreign key is missing in Silver (strict, no ratio tolerance)

Key configuration: - gold_column: foreign key column in Gold table - silver: Silver table location and column - catalog, schema, table, column

Result details: orphaned_records=<count>

Strict in Gold

Unlike Silver's referential_integrity, the Gold check has no min_valid_percent: it passes only when zero foreign keys are missing.

Typical use: - Validate Gold references to Silver - Ensure referential integrity - Detect missing reference data

Example:

referential_integrity:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  gold_column: payment_id
  silver:
    catalog: my_catalog
    schema: my_schema_silver
    table: payments
    column: payment_id

Example Output:

Status Details PASS All 5000 FK references valid in catalog.schema.payments FAIL Found 45 orphaned FK values in 'payment_id' (0.9% of 5000)

docs.title: uniqueness
docs.text:
Purpose: Ensures uniqueness of Gold-level keys.

What it does: - Groups by specified columns - Identifies duplicate keys - Fails if duplicates exist

Key configuration: - columns: list of column names that should be unique - threshold (optional): failure tolerance - max_failure_percent: maximum allowed percentage of duplicate keys (0-100) - max_failure_count: maximum allowed number of duplicate keys

Result details (v1.1.0+): - PASS: "All {n} keys unique" - FAIL: "Found {n} duplicate keys ({pct}% of {total})"

Typical use: - Validate business key uniqueness in aggregated data - Ensure aggregation grain is correct - Detect duplicate aggregations

Example:

uniqueness:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  columns: [payment_id]

Example with threshold:

uniqueness:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  columns: [payment_id, date]
  threshold:
    max_failure_percent: 0.5  # Allow up to 0.5% duplicate keys

Example Output:

Status Details PASS All 5000 rows unique on [payment_id] FAIL Found 25 duplicate rows on [payment_id, date] (0.5% of 5000)

docs.title: coverage
docs.text:
Purpose: Validates that Gold metrics sufficiently cover Silver metrics.

What it does: - Aggregates Gold data using provided expression - Aggregates Silver data using provided expression - Joins on specified keys - Validates coverage percentage within tolerance

Key configuration: - gold_expr: SQL expression to aggregate Gold data - gold_join_columns: column, or list of columns, to join Gold data - silver_expr: SQL expression to aggregate Silver data - silver: Silver table location, as a nested block with catalog, schema, table - silver_join_columns: column, or list of columns, to join Silver data (paired by position with gold_join_columns) - tolerance_percent: acceptable coverage gap (default: 1.0%) - name (optional): descriptive name

Result details: coverage=<pct>%; tolerance=<pct>%

Typical use: - Ensure Gold aggregations cover Silver data - Validate data completeness in aggregation - Detect missing data in rollups

Example:

coverage:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  name: orders_n_coverage

  gold_expr: "SUM(orders_n)"
  gold_join_columns: [order_id]

  silver_expr: "COUNT(DISTINCT transaction_id)"
  silver:
    catalog: my_catalog
    schema: my_schema_silver
    table: orders
  silver_join_columns: [order_id]

  tolerance_percent: 5.0

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Coverage OK: gold=15000, silver=15200 (delta 1.3%) PASS All 50 keys within coverage tolerance (5%) FAIL Coverage delta 8.5% exceeds 5% limit FAIL Found 12 keys exceeding 5% tolerance (24% of 50)

docs.title: volume
docs.text:
Purpose: Detects anomalous variations of a volume metric.

What it does: - Operates in two modes: - Historical mode (recommended): compares current metric against historical baseline - Stateless mode: evaluates metric consistency within current run only - Mode is automatically selected based on configuration - Validates volume is within expected tolerance

Key configuration: - metric: SQL expression to compute volume - min_value (optional): minimum allowed value (stateless bounds mode) - max_value (optional): maximum allowed value (stateless bounds mode) - group_by (optional): columns to group by - name (optional): descriptive name; with several volume instances on one table it becomes part of the check ID (volume[name=<name>]), which is what history rows are matched on - history (optional): historical comparison settings - table: history table location - window: number of historical records to consider (default: 7) - min_history: minimum historical records required (default: 3) - tolerance_percent: allowed deviation from the historical baseline (default: 10)

Result details: anomalies=<count>; max_deviation=<pct>%

Typical use: - Detect sudden volume drops or spikes - Validate data pipeline completeness - Monitor metric stability

Example 1: Historical mode

volume:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false

  metric: "COUNT(*)"

  history:
    table: my_dq_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history
    window: 7
    min_history: 3
    tolerance_percent: 20

Example 2: Stateless mode with grouping

volume:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false

  metric: "SUM(orders_n)"
  group_by:
    - order_id

  min_value: 1

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Volume OK: 15000 (within 20% of baseline 14500) PASS Volume OK: 15000 (min=10000, max=20000) FAIL Historical deviation 35.2% exceeds 20% limit FAIL Volume 8500 below minimum 10000 FAIL Volume 25000 above maximum 20000

docs.title: freshness
docs.text:
Purpose: Ensures Gold data is up to date.

What it does: - Computes maximum timestamp value - Compares to current time - Fails if delay exceeds threshold

Key configuration: - timestamp_column: timestamp column to check (TIMESTAMP or DATE; a date is read as midnight UTC of that day) - max_delay_hours: maximum acceptable delay (default: 24)

Result details: latest=<timestamp>; delay_hours=<hours>

Typical use: - Validate Gold tables are updated regularly - Ensure metrics are current - Detect stale aggregations

Example:

freshness:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  timestamp_column: paid_at
  max_delay_hours: 24

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Data fresh: 6.5h old (within 24h limit) FAIL Data age 36.2h exceeds 24h limit FAIL No data found in column 'paid_at'

docs.title: cross_gold
docs.text:
Purpose: Compares metrics across two Gold tables.

What it does: - Evaluates expressions on two Gold tables - Compares computed values - Allows configurable tolerance

Key configuration: - left_table (optional): left Gold table (schema.table format); defaults to the table under validation - right_table: right Gold table (schema.table format) - left_expr: SQL expression for left table - right_expr: SQL expression for right table - tolerance_abs: acceptable absolute difference (default: 0.01)

Result details: difference=<amount>; tolerance=<amount>

Typical use: - Validate consistency across Gold tables - Compare rollups at different grains - Ensure metric alignment

Example:

cross_gold:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  left_table: my_schema_gold.daily_revenue
  right_table: my_schema_gold.monthly_revenue
  left_expr: "SUM(amount)"
  right_expr: "SUM(amount)"
  tolerance_abs: 0.01

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Cross-gold OK: left=150000.00, right=150000.00 (diff=0.00) PASS All 12 groups within tolerance (0.01) FAIL Difference 150.5000 exceeds tolerance 0.01 FAIL Found 3 groups exceeding tolerance 0.01 (25% of 12)

docs.title: completeness
docs.text:
Purpose: Verifies that all expected dimension values are present in the data.

What it does: - Extracts distinct values from a column - Compares against expected values list - Identifies missing and (optionally) extra values

Key configuration: - column: Column containing dimension values (required) - expected_values: List of values that must be present (required) - allow_extra: Allow values not in expected list (default: true)

Result details: expected=<count>; actual=<count>; missing=[...]; extra=[...]

Typical use: - Validate all regions/countries are present - Ensure all product categories exist - Verify rollup completeness

Example:

completeness:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  column: region
  expected_values:
    - "EMEA"
    - "APAC"
    - "AMERICAS"
  allow_extra: false

Example Output:

Status Details PASS All 3 expected values present in 'region' FAIL Completeness issue in 'region': 1 missing FAIL Completeness issue in 'region': 1 missing, 2 unexpected FAIL Column not found: 'region'

docs.title: trend
docs.text:
Purpose: Verifies metric trend compared to historical values.

What it does: - Computes current metric value - Retrieves historical values from DQ history table - Calculates deviation from median baseline - Supports stable, increasing, or decreasing trend directions

Key configuration: - metric: SQL expression for the metric (required) - name: instance label (required); with several trend instances on one table it becomes part of the check ID (trend[name=<name>]). History is matched on that persisted check ID - history: historical comparison settings (required) - table: table containing historical DQ results (required) - window: number of historical records to consider (default: 7) - min_history: minimum records required for comparison (default: 3) - tolerance_percent: allowed percentage deviation from median (default: 20) - direction: Expected trend - "stable", "increasing", "decreasing" (default: stable)

Result details: current=<value>; baseline=<median>; deviation_pct=<pct>; direction=<dir>

Typical use: - Monitor KPI stability over time - Detect unexpected metric changes - Validate growth/decline trends

Example 1: Stable metric

trend:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  metric: "COUNT(*)"
  history:
    table: my_dq_catalog.dq_metadata.dq_test_history
    window: 7
    min_history: 3
    tolerance_percent: 20
  name: daily_record_count
  direction: stable

Example 2: Increasing metric

trend:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  metric: "SUM(revenue)"
  history:
    table: analytics_gold.dq.history
    window: 12
    min_history: 6
    tolerance_percent: 10
  name: monthly_revenue_trend
  direction: increasing

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Trend OK (stable): current=15000, baseline=14800 (deviation 1.4%) PASS Insufficient history (2 < 3), current=15000 FAIL Trend deviation (stable) 28.5% exceeds 20% limit FAIL Trend deviation (increasing) 15.2% exceeds 10% limit

docs.title: distinct_count
docs.text:
Purpose: Validates that the number of distinct values in a column is within expected bounds.

What it does: - Counts distinct values in a column - Compares against expected value or min/max range - Fails if count is outside bounds

Key configuration: - column: Column to count distinct values (required) - expected: Exact expected distinct count (optional) - min_distinct_count: Minimum expected distinct count (optional) - max_distinct_count: Maximum expected distinct count (optional)

Result details: distinct_count=<count>; expected=<value> or distinct_count=<count>; min=<min>; max=<max>

Typical use: - Validate cardinality constraints in aggregated data - Ensure dimension tables have expected entries - Detect data anomalies in rollups

Example:

distinct_count:
  enabled: true
  severity: warning
  blocking: false
  column: product_category
  min_distinct_count: 5
  max_distinct_count: 50

Example Output:

Status Details PASS Distinct count OK: 25 in 'product_category' (min=5, max=50) FAIL Distinct count 3 below minimum 5 FAIL Distinct count 75 above maximum 50

docs.title: json_schema
docs.text:
Purpose: Validates JSON column structure, required fields, field types, and allowed values.

What it does: - Parses JSON column content - Validates required fields exist - Validates field types match expectations - Validates field values are in allowed sets - Supports nested field validation with dot-notation

Key configuration: - column: JSON column name (required) - required_fields: List of fields that must exist (optional, supports dot-notation) - field_types: Dict of field -> expected type (optional) - allowed_values: Dict of field -> allowed value list (optional) - array_element: If true, validates array elements (default: true) - sample_size: Rows to sample for validation (default: 1000, 0 = all) - threshold: Optional threshold configuration - max_failure_percent: Maximum allowed percentage of validation failures (0-100) - max_failure_count: Maximum allowed number of validation failures

Supported types: string, int, long, double, float, boolean

Result details: total_elements=<count>; missing_fields={...}; type_mismatches={...}; invalid_values={...}

Typical use: - Validate aggregated JSON metadata - Ensure configuration columns have correct structure - Validate semi-structured Gold outputs

Example:

json_schema:
  enabled: true
  severity: critical
  blocking: true
  column: summary_metadata
  required_fields:
    - aggregation_type
    - period
    - metrics.count
  field_types:
    period: string
    metrics.count: int
  allowed_values:
    aggregation_type: ["daily", "weekly", "monthly"]

Example Output:

Status Details PASS JSON schema OK: 1000 elements validated FAIL JSON validation failed: 1 missing fields, 2 invalid values in 'summary_metadata' FAIL JSON parse failed: 15 rows (1.5%) exceed 0% limit

docs.title: Do
docs.text:
• Validate business metrics and reconciliation: Gold ensures KPIs are correct
  • Prefer blocking for financial or KPI-critical checks: Use blocking: true for critical metrics
  • Use Silver as authoritative source for reconciliation: Always reconcile Gold aggregations against Silver
  • Validate metric consistency: Ensure derived metrics are correctly calculated

docs.title: Avoid
docs.text:
• Validate row-level correctness: Row-level validation belongs in Silver
  • Skip reconciliation checks: Always validate Gold matches Silver source
  • Ignore historical context: Use volume checks to detect anomalies

docs.title: Conceptual Positioning
docs.text:
Bronze → Silver → Gold

Bronze: Data landed correctly (technical validation)

Silver: Data is correct and consistent (business validation)

Gold: Data supports business decisions (KPI validation)

This separation is intentional and enforced by the framework design.

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
Full Gold configuration for a sales analytics pipeline:

gold:
  # Tables with specific checks
  tables:
    # Payments aggregation table
    - catalog: my_catalog
      schema: my_schema_gold
      table: payments
      checks:
